name: A Tale in the Desert
summary: A combat-free MMO set in ancient Egypt in which players gather, craft, and build, pass tests in several disciplines, and govern the world through player-written petitions and votes, with the world wiped and restarted at the end of each Telling.
core_loop: gather wood, stone, flax, and other materials -> craft tools and build production structures -> pass discipline tests, many involving other players -> propose petitions and vote on laws -> build monuments -> the Telling ends and the world resets
design_notes: ATITD has no combat; competition runs through seven tests in each discipline, some of which require cooperation, voting, or mass participation, and through player-written law. Seven Monuments built by players who reach Oracle rank end the Telling, after which the world is wiped and the next Telling can change the rules. Discipline tests and periodic world resets are not yet mechanics in the taxonomy (proposal seasonal-world-reset).

name: Against the Storm
summary: A roguelite city builder in which each settlement must fill a reputation gauge before the Queen's impatience runs out, balancing three villager species' needs while opening dangerous forest glades under a recurring blightstorm.
core_loop: embark with three species and a few goods -> build camps, production, and housing in a cleared glade -> meet each species' needs to keep it content -> complete orders and open glades for reputation -> win before the Queen's impatience fills -> carry rewards to the Smoldering City
design_notes: Against the Storm compresses a city builder into short runs: each settlement is a fresh generated map with a race between two gauges, reputation that the player fills and the Queen's impatience that fills on its own, and earning reputation also lowers impatience. Each village hosts three of seven species with distinct housing, food, luxury, and recreation preferences, so the same production network must serve conflicting demands. Rewards carry over to upgrade the Smoldering City between runs, a meta-progression system the taxonomy lacks (see run proposal).

name: AI Dungeon
summary: A text adventure in which a large language model continues the story after each player input, so actions, dialogue, and world facts the player types are improvised into narration rather than resolved by authored rules.
core_loop: choose a setting -> type a Do, Say, or Story input -> model continues the text from recent story and pinned memory -> player undoes, retries, or edits the output -> next input
design_notes: At runtime the model does all the work: each turn, the game assembles a prompt from the scenario premise, player-pinned memory, and recent story text, and a language model (GPT-2 with 1.5 billion parameters in AI Dungeon 2, GPT-3 through OpenAI's API for the premium Dragon model from July 2020) generates the next passage. There is no separate world state, inventory, or rules engine, so consistency lasts only as long as facts stay in the context window, and undo, retry, and edit are the player's tools for steering. Nick Walton built the first version at a BYU hackathon on a 126-million-parameter GPT-2 and released it in May 2019; Latitude relaunched it in December 2019. It is a boundary case: no system is simulated outside the model's text.

name: Animal Crossing: New Horizons
summary: A Nintendo life sim on a deserted island whose clock, seasons, and wildlife follow the real calendar, built around gathering, D.I.Y. crafting, museum collections, villager relationships, and island design.
core_loop: visit the island each real day -> gather wood, fruit, fish, bugs, and fossils -> craft D.I.Y. items and spend Bells and Nook Miles -> donate to the museum and decorate -> island rating rises and unlocks services -> new seasons bring new species
design_notes: Time runs on the console clock, and weather, seasons, and species availability follow the hemisphere chosen at start, so a missed month means missing that month's fish and bugs. The developers lowered bank interest and removed waits from landscaping and crafting to reduce the payoff of changing the console clock. The island's one-to-five-star rating gates milestones such as K.K. Slider's concert at three stars, after which the Island Designer lets players add and remove cliffs, water, and paths. The turnip stalk market sells turnips on Sunday mornings, changes buy prices twice daily under one of four weekly patterns, and spoils unsold turnips the next Sunday.

name: Anno 117: Pax Romana
summary: A Roman-era Anno city builder in which residents advance from Liberti to Patricians through categorized needs, buildings affect their neighbors, schools generate research, and modular ships guard multi-island trade.
core_loop: settle Latium or Albion and house Liberti -> meet categorized needs with multi-island production chains -> residences advance toward Patricians -> schools produce research and temples belief -> ships carry goods on tracked routes -> defend routes and provinces
design_notes: Anno 117 loosens the strict tier-need ladder: needs fall into categories that can be partly filled, and each good carries attributes with benefits and drawbacks for population, income, health, and satisfaction. Placement matters more than in Anno 1800 because production buildings help or harm nearby structures, paved roads extend building range, and diagonal placement is allowed. Belief tied to chosen gods grants scaling bonuses, a system with no exact taxonomy match (see run proposal).

name: Anno 1800
summary: An industrial-era city builder in which residents advance through five Old World tiers by consuming goods from multi-island production chains, linked to a New World session by trade routes and contested by AI rivals.
core_loop: settle an island and house farmers -> meet tier needs with production chains -> houses advance to workers, artisans, engineers, and investors -> higher tiers need goods from other islands and the New World -> build ships and trade routes -> expand under rival pressure
design_notes: Demand is generated by population tiers: basic needs raise how many residents a house holds, luxury needs raise taxes and happiness, and a house advances only when full, supplied, and given construction materials, so each new tier opens a new set of chains. Each tier also staffs its own buildings, so advancing workers to artisans removes labor from worker-tier factories. Old World cities depend on goods from a parallel New World session, so ship routes between sessions are a logistics layer on top of island production.

name: Arma 3
summary: A first-person military simulation on large open terrains in which infantry, vehicles, and aircraft fight under modeled ballistics, recoil, and load-based stamina, extended by the Eden editor, SQF scripting, and a large mod community.
core_loop: load a scenario or join a server -> move and coordinate as infantry or vehicle crew -> spot and engage under ballistics and recoil -> manage load, stamina, and wounds -> complete objectives or die -> build and share new scenarios
design_notes: Arma 3 treats the battlefield as a sandbox: large terrains of up to 163 square kilometers host infantry, vehicles, and aircraft under the same ballistic rules, and scenarios define the war. Much of its life comes from community scenarios and mods built with the Eden editor and SQF scripting, while Bohemia's military consultants reviewed its Tac-Ops missions. Projectile ballistics is not yet a mechanic in the taxonomy (proposal projectile-ballistics).

name: Aurora 4X
summary: A free space 4X simulation by a single developer in which the player runs an interstellar empire through ship design from components, mineral mining, sensor-based detection, missile and beam combat, and named officers, with time advanced in steps from seconds to days.
core_loop: survey bodies and jump points -> mine Trans-Newtonian minerals and build installations -> research components -> design ship classes -> build fleets and assign officers -> detect and fight with sensors, missiles, and beams -> colonize and expand
design_notes: Aurora began as a helper program for the Starfire board wargame and grew into a standalone simulation with no fixed goals. It exposes almost every subsystem as windows of numbers, from mineral accessibility to officer bonuses and ship maintenance. Time advances in player-chosen steps from 5 seconds to 30 days, so the same engine resolves both strategic expansion and individual missile salvos. The Visual Basic 6 original was superseded by a C# rewrite released in 2020.

name: Autonauts
summary: A colony automation game in which the player crafts workerbots from parts and teaches them farming, crafting, and cooking routines in a Scratch-style visual language, so that bots supply the food, housing, and care that a growing population of Folk needs.
core_loop: gather sticks and stone by hand -> craft tools and a workerbot -> teach the bot a task by demonstrating it -> edit the visual script into a loop -> chain bots into farming, crafting, and cooking lines -> supply Folk with food, housing, and care -> unlock new buildings and bot parts
design_notes: Autonauts, from Denki and designers Gary Penn and Aaron Puzey, makes automation a matter of teaching: the player performs an action while a bot watches, the bot records it as blocks in a Scratch-style visual language, and the player adds repeat loops and conditions so the routine runs unattended. Programs are bounded by bot hardware: the head sets maximum instructions (12 at Mk 0 to 32 at Mk 3, raised by brain upgrades) and search range, the body sets hand, backpack, and upgrade slots, and the drive sets speed, battery, and recharge time, so better routines need better-built bots. Folk are the demand side, consuming food that lasts from 10 seconds for water to 120 seconds for apple pie or cooked fish and needing housing and baths, and they are either fully happy or unhappy. Colonise mode introduces components step by step, while Free and Creative modes unlock everything.

name: Balance of Power
summary: A Cold War geopolitical sim in which the player, as US or Soviet leader, spends aid, treaties, and interventions on minor countries over eight annual turns and manages escalating crises to gain prestige without triggering nuclear war.
core_loop: review the world map and country data -> commit aid, treaties, and interventions -> rival superpower responds -> contested moves become crises -> escalate or back down -> prestige shifts -> next annual turn
design_notes: Crawford built the game around country-level state (alignment, government stability, insurgency) that responds to superpower actions, and around a two-sided crisis exchange in which backing down costs prestige and pushing too far ends the game in nuclear war. Ending the game at nuclear war, rather than letting the war be fought, is its main difference from Bruce Ketchledge's Geopolitique 1990. The crisis escalation exchange is not yet a mechanic in the taxonomy (proposal crisis-escalation).

name: Banished
summary: A survival city builder without money or a tech tree in which exiled families gather, farm, and stockpile for winter while aging, births, disease, and disasters decide whether the town grows or starves.
core_loop: assign citizens to gathering, farming, and building jobs -> stockpile food, firewood, and tools for winter -> families form when housing exists and children grow into workers -> aging, disease, and disasters remove citizens -> expand or collapse
design_notes: Citizens are the main resource: every worker is a person who was born, ages, needs a house to start a family, and dies, so the town's age structure produces labor booms and busts years after a decision. There is no money and no tech tree; any building is available once its resources exist, and trade is barter with visiting ships that can also bring disease. Designer Luke Hodorowicz cited the Anno series as a big inspiration and left combat out, and the genre literature credits Banished with starting the survival city-builder trend.

name: BeamNG.drive
summary: A vehicle sim built on soft-body physics in which every vehicle is a node-and-beam skeleton that flexes, deforms, and breaks under impact, played as a free-roam sandbox with scenarios.
core_loop: pick a vehicle and map -> drive, race, or stage a crash -> node-beam structure deforms and parts fail -> inspect the damage -> reset or change vehicle, conditions, or mods
design_notes: Vehicles are defined in JBeam, a JSON format of nodes and beams, and the same structure produces both handling and damage: frames flex, doors detach, windows shatter, tires blow, engines degrade, and fuel tanks can explode. Free roam exposes simulation parameters (time, gravity, wind), so much play is experiment rather than goal. Lua scripting and an official in-game mod repository make the vehicle and scenario set community-driven, and BeamNG.tech forks the engine for education and research.

name: Besiege
summary: A physics construction game where the player builds medieval siege machines from blocks, wheels, and weapons, then drives them against castles and armies in objective levels or a sandbox.
core_loop: read the level objective -> attach blocks, wheels, hinges, and weapons to a starting block -> bind controls -> run the level and drive the machine -> watch it work, flip, or break apart -> revise the design
design_notes: Machines grow from a single starting block, and each attached block is a rigid body joined to its neighbor by a breakable joint; powered wheels, hinges, pistons, and springs are bound to player keys, so a machine is both a structure and a control scheme. Designs fail by tipping, tearing at weak joints, or setting themselves alight, which is much of the appeal. Logic blocks (timers, logic gates, sensors) added later let machines act without input, and the level editor and PC multiplayer turned designs into contests.

name: Big Ambitions
summary: A business life sim set in a simulated New York City in which the player's avatar rents storefronts, stocks and staffs shops, builds warehouse logistics, and grows from one store into a business empire.
core_loop: rent a building and renovate it -> buy stock and set prices -> customers visit and buy -> hire staff and managers -> import from the harbour into warehouses -> trucks deliver to stores -> invest profits in more businesses and real estate
design_notes: Big Ambitions starts the business at street level: the avatar personally rents, furnishes, stocks, and runs the first store and must also eat, sleep, and stay healthy and happy. Growth comes from replacing the player's own labor with staff and then with managers (HR managers, logistics managers, purchasing agents) who automate hiring, purchasing, and delivery from an HQ. Supply moves through a physical chain from harbour importers to warehouses to stores on delivery trucks. Business types range from gift shops and supermarkets to law firms and web development.

name: Big Pharma
summary: A pharmaceutical factory and business sim in which the player routes ingredients through machines on conveyor belts to push their concentration into the range that activates cures while suppressing side effects, then sells into contested markets.
core_loop: import an ingredient -> route it through machines that change its concentration -> activate cures and remove side effects -> form pills and ship them -> grade and price against market demand and rivals -> research better machines
design_notes: Big Pharma's production puzzle is numeric: each ingredient carries cures and side effects that are active only inside concentration windows on a 0 to 20 scale, and machines raise, lower, combine, or transform effects at set concentrations. A line is a sequence of machines on conveyor belts in a fixed floor plan, so the order of operations and the space they take are both constraints. Products are graded from effectiveness, side effects, and market demand, and rival companies release competing drugs that saturate a disease's market. The primary challenge is line layout rather than corporate strategy, which places it in the factory-automation lineage with a business layer.

name: Bitburner
summary: A free, open-source incremental hacking game in which the player writes JavaScript scripts that hack, grow, and weaken simulated servers for money, then spends it with faction reputation on augmentations that reset progress in exchange for permanent multipliers.
core_loop: write a script -> gain root on servers -> run hack, grow, and weaken threads -> earn money and hacking experience -> buy RAM and programs -> gain faction reputation -> buy augmentations and install them, resetting progress -> destroy a BitNode for a Source-File and start the next
design_notes: Bitburner is an incremental game whose economy is a small numerical model the player automates in code. Each server holds a money stock and a security level: hack() steals a percentage of the money and raises security, grow() multiplies money back and also raises security, and weaken() lowers security toward a floor of max(1, round(starting security / 3)), with hack chance and timing set by security and the player's hacking level. Writing schedulers that balance these three calls across many servers and threads is the main skill. Progress is layered by resets: augmentations bought with money and faction reputation (each purchase doubling later prices) take effect only when installed, which wipes most progress, and destroying a BitNode by hacking w0r1d_d43m0n at hacking level 3000 resets further but grants a permanent Source-File. This prestige-reset structure has no taxonomy entry, so this run proposed one. Later BitNodes add systems such as Bladeburner and sleeves.

name: Black & White
summary: A god game in which the player wins villagers' belief through miracles, help, or fear while training a giant creature whose behavior is learned from the player's rewards and punishments.
core_loop: impress villagers with miracles, help, or fear -> belief grows and worship generates prayer power -> cast miracles with the Hand and gestures -> train the creature with strokes and slaps -> the creature acts on learned desires -> convert rival villages and move to the next island
design_notes: Richard Evans built the creature on a belief-desire-intention model after Bratman: beliefs are lists of data about world objects, desires are simplified perceptrons, and opinions are decision trees about how to satisfy a desire; the creature picks the belief with the best opinion for each desire as its intention, and strokes and slaps adjust those opinions by reinforcement. A leash directs the creature's attention so it can learn by observation. The player's actions also move a good-evil alignment that changes the land, interface, music, and followers' view of the god, with a good and an evil advisor arguing each case; alignment has no mechanic id yet (proposal filed). The interface is an animated hand that throws objects and casts gestures instead of icons and panels.

name: Caesar III
summary: A Roman city builder in which service walkers roam the roads from their buildings, houses evolve only where food, goods, and services actually reach them, and missions are won on culture, prosperity, peace, and favor ratings.
core_loop: place housing plots and roads -> walkers from service buildings roam the roads and cover the houses they pass -> houses evolve when food, goods, and services reach them -> taxes and trade fund the city -> raise culture, prosperity, peace, and favor ratings to win the mission
design_notes: Coverage is delivered by individual walkers whose routes depend on road layout, so the same buildings serve a block well or badly depending on junctions; the developers cited SimCity's static placement as what they wanted to make less static. In the logic preserved by the Julius re-implementation, a walker sets a house's coverage to 96 and coverage decays by 1 per update, while prefects zero fire risk and engineers zero collapse risk. City and empire share one map, and gods that punish neglect have no matching taxonomy mechanic (see run proposal).

name: Capitalism
summary: A corporate business sim in which the player builds retail stores, factories, farms, mines, and R&D centers from internal unit layouts and competes with AI firms on price, quality, and brand across city markets.
core_loop: buy land and place a firm -> lay out its internal units -> link purchasing, manufacturing, and sales units into supply chains -> set prices and advertising -> compete for market share on price, quality, and brand -> reinvest, research, or trade stock
design_notes: Trevor Chan's Capitalism models a firm as a small grid of internal units (purchasing, manufacturing, sales, advertising) that the player wires together, so every factory, farm, mine, and store is a layout and logistics puzzle inside a market model. Retail is the main income source: each department store sells up to four products, and customers weigh price, product quality, and brand against competing stores. R&D centers raise product quality over projects lasting from six months to ten years, and AI rivals can be set from aggressive to conservative. An optional stock market allows takeovers, and hired presidents can run divisions. Advertising spend that builds brand awareness has no mechanic in the taxonomy (proposed as advertising-awareness).

name: Captain of Industry
summary: An industrial colony builder in which the player reshapes island terrain with excavators and trucks, runs production chains to feed, house, and power a settlement, and spends the Unity its satisfied population generates on edicts, quick builds, and world-map expansion.
core_loop: designate mining and dumping areas -> trucks haul ore and rock -> smelt and refine into goods -> feed, power, and house the population -> satisfied needs generate Unity -> spend Unity and products on research, edicts, and ship expeditions -> expand and terraform
design_notes: Captain of Industry joins a factory game to a settlement whose population is both labor and a consumer: residents need housing, food, water, electricity, healthcare, and household goods, each fully satisfied need yields about one to two Unity per month, and Unity buys edicts, outposts, quick trades, instant construction, and emergency repairs. Every working vehicle and many buildings consume crafted Maintenance I, II, or III; below 75% a monthly breakdown roll begins, reaching 50% at zero, so maintenance is itself a production chain whose failure cascades through the economy. Terrain is a stock of materials: excavators dig inside a Mine Control Tower's area, trucks dump rock and dirt that settle at per-material angles of repose (about 42 degrees for loose dirt to 78 for hardened rock), and dumping reclaims ocean for ports. A ship explores a world map for islands, refugees, and trade partners. Unity works like a political-capital currency earned from welfare, which the taxonomy lacks; this run proposed one.

name: Car Mechanic Simulator 2021
summary: A first-person garage sim in which the player diagnoses and repairs customer cars part by part, restores auction and barn-find cars, and expands the workshop.
core_loop: accept a generated customer order -> inspect and test the car -> remove parts in order to reach faulty ones -> buy or repair replacements -> reassemble and test drive -> get paid -> upgrade the garage and restore cars for sale
design_notes: The car is a tree of modeled parts (over 4000 across 72 cars) with a removal order, so labor is spent reaching a faulty component before replacing it, the series loop carried over from Car Mechanic Simulator 2018. Customer orders are generated without end, while story missions, car and salvage auctions, barn finds, and a project-car restoration supply variety. A skills and garage-upgrade system gates faster or more capable work.

name: Caves of Qud
summary: A science-fantasy roguelike RPG with simulated factions, liquids, body parts, and procedurally generated histories, built partly with wave function collapse.
core_loop: explore generated and handmade zones -> fight, trade, and talk with faction members -> mutate and equip -> uncover generated history -> go deeper
design_notes: A roguelike included for its simulation layers: faction reputation that every creature carries, liquids that mix and flow, body-part anatomy, and procedurally generated sultan histories that the world refers to. It is a frequently cited example of wave function collapse in a shipped game.

name: Cities: Skylines
summary: A city builder in which road-following zones, agent citizens who route to work along computed paths, district policies, and player-drawn transit lines make traffic flow the central design problem.
core_loop: draw roads and zone along them -> citizens move in, commute, and shop along computed routes -> population milestones unlock services and map tiles -> set district policies, taxes, and budgets -> fix traffic with road hierarchy and transit -> expand
design_notes: Colossal Order carried the road and transit systems of its Cities in Motion series into a full city builder, so every citizen and vehicle is an agent taking the fastest route and congestion is read directly from visible jams. Zoning cells are generated along whatever road geometry the player draws, freeing layouts from a fixed grid, and districts let the player apply policies and tax rates to painted areas. Paradox approved the project after the reception of SimCity (2013), the game was built for Steam Workshop mods, and widely used mods replace core systems such as traffic rules.

name: Cities: Skylines II
summary: The sequel to Cities: Skylines, with citizens choosing routes by time, comfort, and money, a tech tree of development points, preset climates with seasons, and maps of up to 441 tiles.
core_loop: zone and draw roads -> citizens choose homes, jobs, and routes by cost, time, and comfort -> taxes and fees fund services -> milestones grant development points and map tiles -> unlock transport and services -> expand
design_notes: Route choice is a weighted cost over time, comfort, money, and behavior, so parking fees, transit fares, and lane choice shift where agents go, and the first game's cap of about 65,000 rendered citizens is replaced by a hardware limit. One in-game day and night stands for a month, so daily traffic rhythms and seasonal climate run on different scales. The launch drew criticism for performance and its economy simulation, console versions were delayed indefinitely in 2024, and development moved from Colossal Order to Iceflake Studios after a November 2025 announcement.

name: Sid Meier's Civilization
summary: A turn-based 4X game in which the player guides a civilization from 4000 BC toward the space age by founding cities, researching a technology tree, building one-per-world wonders, and competing with rival civilizations by diplomacy or war.
core_loop: explore with units -> found and grow cities -> allocate production and research -> unlock advances and wonders -> expand, trade, or fight rivals -> win by conquest or the space race
design_notes: Meier and Shelley combined the technology tree of Francis Tresham's board game with Empire's exploration and conquest and Railroad Tycoon's idea of several interacting systems managed at once; a SimCity-style zoning layer in an early prototype was dropped. Each city works surrounding terrain tiles for food, production, and trade, a worked-tile yield model the taxonomy does not yet name (proposal worked-tile-yields), and battles resolve from unit attack and defense values (proposal stat-combat-resolution). Wonders exist once per world, so building one denies it to every rival.

name: Command: Modern Operations
summary: A real-time operational military simulation in which the player commands air, naval, and land units drawn from a database of tens of thousands of real platforms, sensors, and weapons on a map of Earth, managing doctrine, emissions control, and missions.
core_loop: read the scenario briefing -> set doctrine, emissions control, and weapon release authority -> assign units to patrol, strike, and support missions -> sensors detect and classify contacts -> weapons engage under doctrine -> adjust missions as detections and losses accrue
design_notes: CMO simulates the sensor and weapon chain rather than abstract unit strengths: detection depends on radar propagation, terrain, thermal layers, and weather, and engagement depends on database specifications and doctrine. The player works mostly at mission and doctrine level and lets tactical AI fly and fight, so one player can run scenarios from patrol-boat skirmishes to global war. The Command engine also has a Professional Edition with full database editing, umpire-controlled multiplayer, and Monte Carlo analysis, sold to defense organizations.

name: Contraband Police
summary: A first-person border-post sim set in 1981 in which the player checks drivers' documents, searches vehicles for hidden contraband, chases smugglers, and upgrades the post against gang attacks.
core_loop: check documents -> search the vehicle with UV light and tools -> extract contraband or approve -> arrest or chase fleeing smugglers -> earn cash -> upgrade the post, cars, and defenses -> story missions and raids
design_notes: It moves the Papers, Please inspection loop into a 3D first-person space: document discrepancies are found on paper, but contraband is found physically by examining the vehicle with a UV flashlight and extracting it with tools. The number of documents per entrant grows over time, raising the error rate at constant attention. Inspection income funds post upgrades whose maintenance costs rise, while authored special assignments, chases, and gang raids interrupt the shift loop.

name: Creatures
summary: An artificial-life game in which the player hatches and raises Norns whose neural-network brains, simulated biochemistry, and haploid digital genomes produce learned behavior and heritable mutation.
core_loop: hatch eggs -> Norns act on biochemical drives -> player rewards, punishes, and teaches words -> neural weights shift toward drive-reducing actions -> Norns breed and pass mutated genomes -> next generation behaves differently
design_notes: Steve Grand built each Norn as a stack of coupled models rather than a scripted pet: a neural network whose sight neurons are grouped one per object type, a biochemistry of chemicals and organs that sets drive levels, and a haploid genome with no dominance that codes for both. Learning is behaviorist: high drive levels act as punishment and reductions as reward, so the player's tickles and slaps only matter through the same chemistry. Because the genome builds the brain and body, mutations produce Norns that cannot see, lack organs, or never die, which the online breeding community catalogued and traded. Norns live about 40 hours, short enough for many generations.

name: Crusader Kings III
summary: A character-driven grand strategy game in which the player rules as successive heads of a medieval dynasty from 867 or later to 1453, managing traits, stress, vassal opinion, marriages, and succession across a map of feudal titles.
core_loop: play the current ruler -> manage vassal opinion, council, and stress -> arrange marriages, schemes, and wars over claims -> ruler dies -> heir inherits titles under succession law -> realm fragments or consolidates
design_notes: CK3 makes the player a character rather than a state: realm strength depends on vassals whose itemized opinions, traits, and family ties decide whether they serve or rebel. Succession laws make death the main source of disruption, and stress penalizes playing a character against type, which pushes players to roleplay their traits. Event content is authored but fired from on_actions and character state, so the same templates produce different stories in different courts; culture and religion conversion is not yet a mechanic in the taxonomy (proposal culture-religion-conversion).

name: DCS World
summary: A combat flight sim platform of study-level aircraft modules with clickable cockpits and modeled subsystems, flown in missions and on multiplayer servers built with a Lua-scriptable mission editor.
core_loop: pick a module and mission -> cold start through cockpit switches -> fly and navigate -> find targets with sensors -> employ weapons and survive defenses -> recover and land -> debrief
design_notes: DCS treats each aircraft as a set of subsystems (engines, fuel, electrical, hydraulics, radios, sensors) operated through individually clickable cockpit controls, so procedures and failures follow from system state rather than scripts. Its fidelity reaches professional use: the U.S. Air Force's 355th Training Squadron has used the A-10C module, and French and Ukrainian pilots have trained on modules. The business model is a free base with two aircraft and two maps, with paid aircraft and map modules from Eagle Dynamics and third parties sharing one client.

name: Democracy 4
summary: A turn-based government sim in which the player, as leader of a democracy, adjusts policy sliders whose weighted effects move statistics and overlapping voter groups, resolves dilemmas, and tries to balance the budget and win the next election.
core_loop: spend political capital to adjust policy sliders -> effects propagate through the weighted policy network -> statistics, situations, and voter group happiness shift -> resolve dilemmas and events -> make election promises -> win or lose the election
design_notes: Democracy 4 models a country as one visible causal graph: policies, statistics, situations, and voter groups are nodes, and the interface shows the weighted links in and out of each. The player is constrained by political capital, earned through loyal ministers and spent on policy changes, and by voters who belong to several groups at once. Political capital as a regenerating action currency is not yet a mechanic in the taxonomy (proposal political-capital).

name: Don't Starve
summary: A survival sim in a procedurally generated wilderness where the player balances hunger, health, and sanity, crafts tools and light, and prepares for darkness, hounds, and seasons.
core_loop: explore a generated world by day -> gather and craft tools, food, and light -> manage hunger, health, and sanity -> survive nights, hounds, and seasons -> build a base and stockpile for winter -> die and start a new world
design_notes: Three meters interact: empty hunger drains health, and sanity falls at dusk and night and from unpleasant actions until, below 15% of maximum, shadow creatures attack, so the mind is a survival stock alongside the body. The 8-minute day is divided into day, dusk, and night segments whose split shifts with the season, and total darkness is lethal because Charlie attacks anyone without a light. Hound attacks escalate on a schedule tied to days survived, and death deletes the world except through rare resurrection items. Klei released it in beta in 2012 and fully on 23 April 2013.

name: Dwarf Fortress
aliases: Slaves to Armok: God of Blood Chapter II: Dwarf Fortress
summary: A colony sim in which the player directs a fortress of autonomous dwarves inside a procedurally generated world whose history, geology, fluids, bodies, and minds are all simulated.
core_loop: embark and dig -> designate jobs, stockpiles, and workshops -> dwarves self-assign labors and craft -> needs, emotions, and stress accumulate -> migrants, caravans, sieges, and beasts arrive -> fortress thrives or collapses into the world's legends
design_notes: Tarn Adams's stated principles are to break a system into parts, avoid overplanning, and base each model on a real-world analog; he describes the game as a story generator. The fortress is embarked inside a world whose geology and history were already simulated, and the fortress's own events flow back into that history through Legends, so a collapse becomes a record that a later adventurer can visit. Strange moods let an inspired dwarf seize a workshop to make a named artifact and go insane if materials are missing, which turns the production system into a story source. The game was free and donation-funded from 2006; a paid Steam edition with sprite graphics followed in December 2022, still short of a 1.0 version.

name: Dyson Sphere Program
summary: A 3D factory automation game in which the player's mech builds production lines on rotating planets, links star systems with logistics drones and warp vessels, and launches sails and rockets to assemble Dyson spheres around stars.
core_loop: mine planetary veins -> belt ores through smelters and assemblers -> craft matrix cubes for research -> link planets and stars with logistics stations -> launch solar sails and carrier rockets -> Dyson sphere power feeds endgame production
design_notes: Dyson Sphere Program scales the factory puzzle from one map to a randomly generated cluster of stars: each planet is a rotating sphere whose day-night cycle affects solar power, and logistics stations match per-item local and remote supply and demand, sending up to 100 drones within a planet and 10 vessels between planets or, with Space Warpers, between stars. The Dyson sphere is a megastructure designed in a node-and-frame editor and built by ejecting solar sails (36 kW each at base, scaled by star luminosity, expiring after 5,400 seconds unless captured by a completed shell) and launching carrier rockets; ray receivers return its energy to planets or convert it to critical photons. The December 2023 Dark Fog update added hives and planetary bases whose threat rises with the player's power generation and combat, a variant of pollution-driven aggression. The developers drew inspiration from Stellaris, which included Dyson sphere construction. The sphere works as a goal sink that absorbs very large quantities of sails and rockets; no taxonomy mechanic covers such megaproject sinks, so this run proposed one.

name: Eco
summary: A multiplayer civilization survival game in which players on one server share a simulated ecosystem, specialize in skills, craft and trade with player-made currencies, and pass enforceable laws while researching how to stop a meteor due in thirty days without wrecking the environment.
core_loop: gather from the shared ecosystem -> specialize in skills and craft at tables -> trade through player stores and currencies -> propose and vote on laws and taxes -> research technology to stop the meteor -> manage pollution and species populations before impact
design_notes: Eco makes the ecosystem a shared commons: each player's harvesting and pollution changes species populations and the climate for everyone on the server. Its answer to overexploitation is player-made institutions rather than designer rules, with enforceable laws, taxes, and currencies, and simulation data that players can cite as evidence in debates. It began as an educational project funded in part by the U.S. Department of Education.

name: Elite
summary: A 3D space trading and combat game in which the player flies a single ship through eight seed-generated galaxies, buying and selling cargo and fighting pirates and police to raise a combat rating.
core_loop: buy cargo at a station -> hyperspace to a system within fuel range -> fight or evade pirates and police -> dock by matching the station's rotation -> sell for profit -> buy weapons and equipment -> raise combat rating
design_notes: Each of the eight galaxies and its 256 systems is regenerated from a seed rather than stored, which let a large universe fit in an 8-bit micro and made procedural generation the core of the design. Commodity prices differ by system, and fuel limits each hyperjump to 7 light years, so route choice is the main economic decision. The goal of reaching the Elite combat rank is open-ended; the player chooses between trading, piracy, bounty hunting, and mining.

name: Elite Dangerous
summary: An online space sim set in a 1:1 procedurally generated Milky Way where players trade, fight, mine, and explore while a server-side background simulation shifts faction control from aggregate player actions.
core_loop: take missions or cargo at a station -> jump between star systems -> trade, fight, mine, or explore -> earn credits, rank, and faction influence -> outfit or buy ships -> background simulation shifts faction control and system states
design_notes: Stellar Forge generates around 400 billion star systems from rules of star and planet formation and blends in about 150,000 systems from real astronomical data, so the galaxy is mostly unvisited. The server-side Background Simulation tracks minor-faction influence, economy, and states per system and updates them from what all players do, so Solo, Private Group, and Open players share one political map. Ship capability comes from outfitting modules within power and mass limits, and flight is Newtonian with a default flight-assist layer.

name: Equilinox
summary: A relaxed nature-building game in which the player spreads biomes with grasses, places plants and animals that each have environmental requirements, and spends diversity points earned by healthy species on evolutions and genetic modifications.
core_loop: plant grasses to spread biomes -> place plants and animals whose requirements are met -> healthy species live longer, breed, and earn diversity points -> spend points on new species, genetic modifications, and evolutions -> complete tasks for rewards
design_notes: Equilinox, built solo by ThinMatrix, ties its economy to ecological fit: each species has a life cycle and requirements, and healthy individuals live longer, breed more, and yield more diversity points, the currency for new species and modifications. Evolution is a gated unlock (meet a species' evolution conditions, then pay to evolve) rather than simulated selection, which keeps the 120+ species on an authored progression. Biomes spread from planted grasses, so terrain type is itself a player-placed stock. Paid genetic modification matches the genome-modification proposal from run catalog-ge.

name: Euro Truck Simulator 2
summary: A truck driving sim in which the player hauls timed cargo deliveries across a scaled European road network and grows a transport company of trucks, garages, and hired drivers.
core_loop: take a cargo job -> couple the trailer -> drive the route paying fuel and tolls -> deliver on time with little damage -> earn money and experience -> spend skill points and buy trucks, garages, and drivers -> longer and riskier jobs
design_notes: The pleasure is long-haul driving through a compressed map (71 cities in 12 countries in the base game), with economic pressure from delivery deadlines, fuel, tolls, and repair costs and with damage deducted from pay. Progression is a skill-point tree that unlocks cargo classes (ADR hazardous, long distance, valuable, fragile, urgent, eco driving), plus a company layer in which owned garages host hired AI drivers who earn money off-screen. Multiplayer began as the fan mod TruckersMP in 2013 before official support in 2021.

name: Europa Universalis IV
summary: A real-time-with-pause grand strategy game in which the player directs one of over 500 nations from 1444 to 1821 through monarch-point spending, trade-node competition, colonization, diplomacy, and war on a province map.
core_loop: accrue administrative, diplomatic, and military monarch points -> buy technology, stability, ideas, and development -> steer trade and colonize -> ally and declare wars -> occupy and annex provinces -> manage unrest, estates, and coalitions
design_notes: EU4 converts ruler quality into three spendable currencies (administrative, diplomatic, and military monarch points) that buy technology, stability, ideas, and province development, which makes each succession an economic event. Expansion is checked by systems rather than scripts: aggressive expansion feeds defensive coalitions, and conquered provinces stay restless until integrated. Monarch points, war score, province integration, and missionary conversion are not yet mechanics in the taxonomy (proposals political-capital, war-score-peace, territorial-claims-integration, culture-religion-conversion).

name: EVE Online
summary: A single-universe space MMO in which players mine, manufacture, trade, and fight in ships that are destroyed for good, inside a player-made economy and a galaxy of high-, low-, and null-security space where player alliances claim sovereignty.
core_loop: train skills in real time -> mine, salvage, or run missions for materials and ISK -> manufacture or buy ships and modules on the player market -> fit ships and fly into space of a chosen security level -> lose ships in combat and replace them -> corporations and alliances fight over sovereignty
design_notes: EVE keeps one economy for all players: nearly everything is player-made and ship losses are permanent, so wars create manufacturing demand. Risk and reward are tied to space security, with the most profitable activities in low-sec and null-sec, where the NPC police do not destroy aggressors. CCP hired an economist in 2007 to oversee the economy. Security-graded zones and permanent asset loss on destruction are not yet mechanics in the taxonomy (proposals pvp-security-zones, loss-on-death).

name: Façade
summary: A free 2005 interactive drama in which the player types natural language as a dinner guest of the married couple Grace and Trip while a drama manager sequences authored beats toward one of three endings.
core_loop: type to or touch Grace and Trip -> parser maps input to a discourse act -> characters react and tension shifts -> drama manager picks the next beat -> secrets surface -> the couple reconciles, splits, or throws the player out
design_notes: Michael Mateas and Andrew Stern built Façade as a research artifact: Grace and Trip are written in A Behavior Language (ABL) as reactive behaviors, and a drama manager picks the next story beat from an authored library to follow a tension arc toward a climax. Typed text is mapped to a small set of discourse acts (the Versu paper counts 30 parameterized speech acts and 27 beats), which lets a limited body of authored dialogue answer open-ended input. It is a boundary case: the simulated systems are the parser, character behaviors, and beat sequencing over mostly authored dialogue, built for replay so players can find other outcomes.

name: Factorio
summary: A factory automation game in which the player builds belt, train, robot, and circuit networks that mine, refine, and assemble items on an alien planet while pollution provokes native biters that evolve over time.
core_loop: mine ore -> smelt and assemble on belts and inserters -> feed science packs to labs -> research new machines -> pollution draws biter attacks -> defend and expand outposts by rail -> launch a rocket
design_notes: Lead designer Michal Kovarik cited the Minecraft tech mods IndustrialCraft and BuildCraft; Factorio turned their pipes and machines into a standalone game where ratio planning and layout are the challenge. Item movement is discrete and deterministic (belts carry 15, 30, 45, or 60 items per second across two lanes), which makes throughput legible and lets the lockstep multiplayer simulate identical worlds. Pollution couples industry to combat: chunks above 15 units diffuse 2% to neighbors, spawners that absorb it send attack groups, and total pollution produced drives the enemy evolution factor. Each layer of logistics (belts, trains with block signals, roboport-based logistic and construction robots, circuit combinators) is a mechanic the player adopts when the previous one stops scaling, and blueprints let solved layouts be reused. Speed, productivity, and efficiency modules and beacons that trade power for throughput, and the rocket silo as a terminal sink for produced parts, have no taxonomy entry; this run proposed both.

name: Farming Simulator 25
summary: The 2024 entry in Giants Software's series in which the player runs a farm business by operating over 400 licensed vehicles and implements across seasonal field work, livestock, forestry, and production chains.
core_loop: buy fields and machinery -> plow, seed, fertilize, and harvest with implements -> store or sell crops or feed productions and animals -> take contracts for extra income -> reinvest in land, buildings, and equipment
design_notes: Farming Simulator models agriculture as ordered field operations performed with specific implements, so the challenge is machine operation and fleet logistics rather than market strategy. FS25 lists 25 crop types including two rice varieties grown in paddies, spinach, peas, and green beans, adds water buffalo and goats, adds twisters and hail that damage crops, and deforms soft ground under tires. Dynamically generated contracts pay for work on other farms, and the in-game ModHub distributes developer-tested community vehicles, maps, and scripts.

name: Farthest Frontier
summary: A frontier-town city builder in which crop rotation, soil fertility, diet variety, clean water, and healers decide whether named diseases spread, while prosperity draws stronger raiders against walled defenses.
core_loop: gather, hunt, forage, and farm -> rotate crops to hold soil fertility -> feed a varied diet and supply clean water, clothing, and healers against disease -> upgrade housing and the town center as desirability rises -> fortify against raiders drawn by prosperity
design_notes: Farthest Frontier makes public health the main failure path: dysentery, cholera, tetanus, rabies, frostbite, and bubonic plague each have causes the player can address with clean water, clothing and shoes, healers, and rat catchers. Farming adds soil state, with 12 crops that must be rotated and fields improved by clearing weeds and rocks, and 19 food types with berries and greens preventing scurvy. Prosperity raises raider strength, so growth itself increases military pressure.

name: Football Manager
summary: A football club management series in which the player sets tactics, training, transfers, and finances while a match engine simulates games from the attributes of players drawn from a researched database of real footballers.
core_loop: scout and sign players -> set tactics and training -> the match engine simulates fixtures from attributes and instructions -> morale, form, and finances shift -> the board and fans judge results -> rebuild the squad over seasons
design_notes: Football Manager simulates the whole football world from a database of real players, staff, and clubs maintained by fan researchers, with tens of thousands of players developing, aging, and moving in loaded leagues. Matches are simulated from player attributes and tactical instructions and shown through a 2D engine in FM 2005 and a 3D engine from FM 2009. Information is uncertain: scouts and analysts reveal attributes and fit, and scout knowledge of an area is tracked (as 0 to 100 percent from FM 2018). Everton agreed in 2008 to use the database for scouting. Contract and transfer talks and the board's job-security judgment have no matching mechanics in the taxonomy (proposed as negotiation and board-confidence). The series began as Championship Manager in 1992 and was relaunched under this name with FM 2005 in 2004.

name: Foundation
summary: A gridless medieval city builder in which painted zones grow homes organically, monuments are assembled from modular parts, and the village advances along Labor, Clergy, or Kingdom estates.
core_loop: paint residential, road, patrol, and forestry zones -> villagers build homes inside them -> assign workers and production chains -> trade with neighbors and pay taxes -> advance Labor, Clergy, or Kingdom estates -> assemble monuments from parts
design_notes: Foundation separates intent from layout: the player paints areas for homes, roads, patrols, and forestry, and housing appears inside them without a grid. Major buildings are not fixed footprints but assemblies of parts, so a monument's function and capacity follow from the modules chosen. Progress runs along three estates, which can be specialized or combined.

name: From Dust
summary: A god game in which the player carries sand, water, and lava across islands whose material simulation erodes, floods, and hardens terrain, protecting a tribe as it founds villages at totems.
core_loop: carry sand, water, and lava with the Breath -> reshape terrain to open paths -> send villagers to totems to found villages -> vegetation spreads across soil -> divert tsunamis, floods, fires, and eruptions -> unlock powers and reach the portal
design_notes: Designed by Eric Chahi and presented as a spiritual successor to Populous, it replaces discrete land raising with a continuous material simulation: water flows and erodes, lava cools into solid rock, and soil lets vegetation spread once a village is founded, fast enough that islands can be reshaped within minutes. The cursor, called the Breath, carries matter and changes appearance to match it, replacing a conventional HUD. Disasters are announced shortly before they hit, so each map alternates between building and short preparation windows.

name: Frostpunk
summary: A survival city builder in which the leader of the last city around a coal generator must keep falling temperatures at bay while signing laws that trade citizens' welfare against productivity under hope and discontent meters.
core_loop: keep the coal generator fueled -> heat districts and insulate buildings as temperatures fall -> assign workers to gather coal, wood, steel, and food -> sign laws that trade welfare for productivity -> balance hope and discontent -> survive the storm
design_notes: The city is radial around one generator that heats a circular area, so layout is a function of heat range and fuel, and a coal shortage or overload can end the run. The Book of Laws sequences laws so that early compromises such as child labor or extended shifts open harsher later options, and Order or Faith paths lead toward totalitarian rule, turning policy into moral pressure tracked by hope and discontent. Building heat versus falling outside temperature has no exact taxonomy mechanic (see run proposal); 11 bit studios cites This War of Mine as the origin of its aim for meaningful entertainment, now applied to a whole society.

name: Frostpunk 2
summary: The sequel to Frostpunk, in which the Steward builds whole districts on the frost and must pass laws through a council of 100 faction delegates while faction tension can escalate into civil war.
core_loop: build food, housing, extraction, and industry districts -> heat districts from the generator -> factions propose ideas and laws -> negotiate council votes -> faction tension rises or falls -> survive whiteouts and found colonies
design_notes: Frostpunk 2 moves from single buildings to districts and from one leader's decree to a council: 100 delegates, each tied to a faction, vote on every proposed law, with 51 votes for most laws and two thirds for laws that expand the Steward's power. Negotiated promises that are not kept anger factions, and tension between factions can escalate into murder and civil war, so the developer describes social survival as more important than environmental threats. Population is handled as district-level aggregates rather than individual workers.

name: FTL: Faster Than Light
summary: A roguelite starship sim where the player allocates reactor power and directs crew through room-level oxygen, fire, breach, and system-damage simulation while fleeing a rebel fleet across eight sectors.
core_loop: jump to a beacon -> resolve an event or fight -> allocate reactor power and direct crew under fire -> repair breaches, fires, and systems -> spend scrap on upgrades -> stay ahead of the rebel fleet to the flagship
design_notes: FTL models a ship as rooms with oxygen levels, doors, systems, and crew positions; hits create breaches, fires, and system damage that crew must walk to and repair, so a combat is a spatial triage problem as well as a damage race. The reactor's power bars are the central budget shared by shields, engines, weapons, oxygen, and medbay, and the player shifts them during paused combat. Manual reactor power allocation and per-system damage that removes capacity until repaired have no dedicated taxonomy ids (power-grid is the closest fit); both are recorded as new-mechanic proposals.

name: Game Dev Tycoon
summary: A game-studio business sim where the player picks topic, genre, and platform for each game, splits development effort across design and technology focus areas, and lives or dies by review scores across the history of the industry.
core_loop: choose topic, genre, platform, and audience -> allocate focus across three development stages -> design and technology points accumulate with bugs -> reviews score the game -> sales and fans -> research, engines, and hires
design_notes: Game Dev Tycoon reduces game making to a configuration problem scored by a hidden market model: each topic and genre pair, each genre and audience pair, and each platform carry fit weights, and each genre favors a particular split of effort across the development stages. Review scores compare the new game against the player's previous best, so the bar rises as the studio improves. A fictional timeline of parody consoles enters and leaves the market from the 1980s onward, which forces platform bets (date-driven availability is proposed as dated-tech-timeline). Greenheart released its own cracked copy in which piracy bankrupts the in-game studio.

name: Conway's Game of Life
summary: A zero-player cellular automaton on an infinite square grid in which each cell lives or dies by the B3/S23 neighbor-count rule, producing gliders, oscillators, and universal computation from a seeded pattern.
core_loop: place live cells on the grid -> apply birth on 3 and survival on 2 or 3 neighbors to every cell at once -> pattern stabilizes, oscillates, dies, or emits gliders -> observe -> edit the seed and rerun
design_notes: Conway's rule is the minimal case of emergence from local update: each cell's next state depends only on how many of its eight neighbors are alive, all cells update simultaneously, and the only input is the initial pattern. The rule is Turing complete, so whether an arbitrary pattern stops changing is undecidable, and decades of discovery (Gosper's period-30 glider gun of November 1970, the R-pentomino's 1,103-generation run) came from players searching seeds. Simulators such as Golly add Hashlife for large time jumps and scripting for rule variants. The rule itself is not yet a mechanic in the taxonomy (proposal cellular-automaton-rule), so the decomposition records seeding, stepping, and run speed.

name: Garry's Mod
summary: A Source engine physics sandbox in which players spawn props, ragdolls, and NPCs, join them with welds and constraints, and script whole new multiplayer game modes in Lua.
core_loop: spawn props, ragdolls, and NPCs -> move and freeze them with the physics gun -> weld, rope, and motor them with the tool gun -> test the contraption or scene -> share it, or play a community game mode built on the same tools
design_notes: Garry's Mod exposes the Source engine's rigid-body physics directly: the physics gun grabs, rotates, and freezes any prop, and the tool gun adds welds, ropes, axles, motors, thrusters, and other constraints, so contraptions are built from rigid bodies and joints. Its larger contribution is that the whole game is scriptable in Lua and servers download addons on join, so most play happens inside player-made game modes such as Trouble in Terrorist Town, Prop Hunt, and DarkRP, and the add-on Wiremod adds sensors and logic gates. Garry's Mod began as a free Half-Life 2 mod in 2004 and became a paid Steam product in 2006.

name: Generative Agents (Smallville)
aliases: Smallville;Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
summary: A research sandbox in which 25 language-model agents in a Sims-like town keep natural-language memory streams, reflect, and plan their days, producing unscripted information spread and social coordination.
core_loop: agents perceive nearby events and objects -> observations enter the memory stream -> retrieve memories by recency, importance, and relevance -> plan the day and react -> converse and act -> reflections summarize memories -> plans and relationships change
design_notes: Park and colleagues replace authored behavior trees with a loop of language-model calls on gpt-3.5-turbo. Every observation is stored as text with timestamps; retrieval scores memories by recency (decay 0.995 per game hour), importance (rated 1-10 by the model when stored), and embedding relevance, each normalized and weighted equally. When the summed importance of recent events passes 150 (two or three times a day) the agent writes reflections, and plans are decomposed from a day outline into hour and 5-15 minute chunks. Seeding one agent with the intent to host a Valentine's Day party led to 13 of 25 agents hearing about it and five attending over two game days, at a cost of thousands of dollars in API credits. The open-source release steps the town 10 game seconds per step.

name: Going Medieval
summary: A colony sim set after a plague in which settlers with traits, needs, and moods dig into and build up a multi-level voxel terrain to survive seasons and raids.
core_loop: dig into and build up voxel terrain -> assign settlers to roles and jobs -> settlers meet needs and mood shifts -> seasons change food supply -> raiders and beasts attack the walls -> research, build higher, and take in newcomers
design_notes: It follows the RimWorld pattern of named settlers with traits, perks, skills, needs, and moods, and is widely compared to RimWorld and Dwarf Fortress. Its distinctive layer is a fully three-dimensional voxel map: the player can dig cellars and caverns, raise multi-storey stone and timber forts, and reshape earth and water, so defensive geometry and storage depth are design problems in three dimensions. Early access ran from June 2021 to the 1.0 release in March 2026.

name: Gran Turismo
summary: A PlayStation racing game that paired a tuned handling model and 140 production cars with license tests, prize credits, and parts tuning in a Simulation mode career.
core_loop: pass license tests -> enter championships -> win credits and prize cars -> buy cars and performance parts -> tune the car -> enter higher-class events
design_notes: Simulation mode made car ownership and driving skill the progression: driver's licenses earned through timed tests gate events, and credits from championships buy cars, parts, and tuning. Reviewers singled out the handling model and the tuning freedom, and criticized license tests that could be harder than the races they unlocked. It was the first game designed for the DualShock's analog control and rumble, and IGN called it the grandfather of modern console racing sims.

name: Gran Turismo 7
summary: A console racing simulator that combines a detailed vehicle dynamics model and car collection with GT Sophy, a deep reinforcement learning opponent added as a permanent rival in 2023.
core_loop: buy or tune a car -> race against AI or players -> earn credits -> expand the collection -> harder events
design_notes: Included because it is the clearest shipped case of a learned opponent in a simulation game. GT Sophy, trained with model-free deep reinforcement learning on parallel simulator instances, became selectable as a permanent rival in 2023 and was extended to custom races in 2025, one content update at a time.

name: Hamurabi
summary: A ten-turn text game in which the player, as the Babylonian king Hammurabi, splits a grain stock between feeding people, planting acres, and buying land while harvests, rats, and plague vary at random.
core_loop: read the steward's yearly report -> trade grain for land at a random price -> allocate grain to food and seed -> harvest, rats, arrivals, and plague resolve -> next year
design_notes: Three stocks (people, acres, bushels of grain) and three yearly allocations make the whole game one stock-and-flow puzzle: grain is food, seed, and the currency for land at once, so every bushel has competing uses. Randomness enters only through harvest yield, rat losses, a land price of 17 to 26 bushels per acre, arrivals, and a plague that halves the population, so the player manages expected value under variance. Dyment wrote it in FOCAL for the PDP-8 from a description of The Sumerian Game (1964); David Ahl's BASIC version spread it as a type-in listing and seeded Kingdom, Dukedom, and Santa Paravia en Fiumaccio.

name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker
summary: A zero-gravity salvage sim in which the player cuts derelict ships apart with a laser cutter and grapple, manages decompression and volatile systems, and sorts salvage to pay down a large debt.
core_loop: start a shift -> scan the ship -> vent pressure and make power, fuel, coolant, and reactor systems safe -> cut parts free -> grapple them to the correct receptacle -> salvage value pays down debt -> buy tool upgrades
design_notes: Each ship is a physics assembly of joined parts and typed hazards rather than an authored level: cutting into a pressurized room causes explosive decompression, cutting live electrical wires or coolant pipes can explode, and a reactor removed from its casing must be delivered before it melts down. The order of disassembly is the puzzle, and the taxonomy lacks a mechanic for it (proposed as salvage-deconstruction). Oxygen and thruster fuel act as survival stocks, and shifts are timed except in Open Shift mode.

name: Harvest Moon
summary: An early farming sim for the Super Famicom in which the player has two and a half years to restore an inherited farm through daily crop watering, livestock care, and courting one of five eligible women.
core_loop: clear land and plant seasonal crops -> water daily and tend livestock -> ship produce for money -> buy animals, seeds, and upgrades -> build relationships and attend festivals -> marry and raise a child before the father's evaluation
design_notes: Director Yasuhiro Wada started the project with three principles (no fighting, uniqueness, and tactile real-time action), and a team of 8 to 10 people at Pack-In-Soft scaled it back to fit SNES limits. The farm rules are forgiving but daily: unwatered crops stop growing instead of dying, chickens need only feed but can die if left outside, and cows must be fed, talked to, brushed, and milked or they sicken. Play is bounded by a two-and-a-half-year term that ends with the father's evaluation of the farm and family, which makes marriage and a child goals alongside crops and livestock.

name: Hearts of Iron IV
summary: A World War II grand strategy game starting in 1936 or 1939 in which the player builds factories, turns resources into equipment, designs divisions, follows a national focus tree, and directs fronts and battle plans across land, sea, and air.
core_loop: pick national focuses and spend political power -> assign civilian factories to construction and military factories to equipment -> design and train divisions -> draw fronts and battle plans -> divisions fight on supply, terrain, and weather -> capitulate rivals or hold
design_notes: HOI4 separates the industrial war from the field war: civilian factories build capacity and military factories turn resources into equipment, so divisions fight only as well as stockpiles and supply allow. Battle plans let the player act at army-group scale and leave division movement to the AI. National focus trees are the authored branching layer that steers countries toward historical or alternate paths, while battles resolve from unit statistics (proposal stat-combat-resolution).

name: House Flipper
summary: A first-person renovation sim in which the player cleans, paints, demolishes, and furnishes rundown houses, then sells them to buyers whose bids depend on how well the house fits their needs.
core_loop: take email jobs for cash -> buy a rundown house -> clean, demolish, paint, tile, furnish -> buyers evaluate fit and bid -> sell at a profit -> buy bigger properties
design_notes: Each property is judged by a small set of buyer profiles with requirements such as cleanliness or a family room, and their auction bids reward matching a profile rather than maximizing generic quality. Labor is performed with coverage tools (paint roller, mop, window cleaner, plaster tool) that show visible progress, and tool use earns experience spent on faster tools. Email jobs paid by size and quality supply the capital for the first purchase.

name: Infinite Craft
summary: A browser crafting game in which combining any two elements yields a new element whose name and emoji a language model generates on first request and a shared database then fixes for all players.
core_loop: start with water, fire, wind, and earth -> drag two elements together -> look up the pair in the shared database -> if new, a language model names the result and picks an emoji -> result is cached for everyone -> combine the new element further
design_notes: At runtime the model is consulted only on a cache miss: the game checks a global database for the unordered pair, and if no result exists, Llama 2 (later Llama 3.1) generates a short element name, capped at twenty tokens, plus an emoji; the result is stored so the same pair returns the same element to every player. The recipe graph is therefore written collectively and lazily by players and the model, and a First Discovery label marks players who triggered a generation. Pairwise combination discovery is not yet a mechanic in the taxonomy (proposal combination-discovery). It is a boundary case: there is no simulated system beyond the generated recipe graph.

name: inZOI
summary: A Krafton life sim in early access since March 2025 in which the player oversees autonomous Zois with eight needs in dense cities, with optional on-device language model prompts and generative tools for patterns and objects.
core_loop: create Zois and build homes -> Zois act on needs and personality -> player directs actions or prompts thoughts -> jobs, relationships, rumors, and illness move through the city -> edit the city and generate new items -> share on Canvas
design_notes: inZOI casts the player as an intern at AR Company who manages a city of virtual people and its karma system. It pairs a Sims-style needs model (hunger, hygiene, bathroom, fun, social, energy, sleep, recognition) with city-scale free will that the developers say produces rumors, trends, and disease, plus optional direct control of a Zoi or vehicle. Generative models sit mainly in the creation layer: text prompts generate patterns and images for clothing and furniture, 2D images convert to 3D props, and an on-device small language model lets typed prompts steer a Zoi's thoughts and actions. City-wide progression of unplayed Zois is the offscreen-life-progression mechanic; karma has no mechanic id.

name: iRacing
summary: A subscription online racing sim with laser-scanned cars and tracks in which drivers race scheduled official series and advance through license classes gated by a no-fault Safety Rating, while an Elo-style iRating sorts fields.
core_loop: join a scheduled official race -> qualify and race on laser-scanned tracks -> incidents and results update Safety Rating and iRating -> license promotion opens higher series -> buy cars and tracks for the next season
design_notes: iRacing grew from Papyrus's NASCAR Racing 2003 Season code with a new tire model and LIDAR-scanned cars and tracks. Its distinctive layer is the competitive structure: a no-fault Safety Rating from incident points per corner gates license classes (Rookie, D, C, B, A, with Pro reserved for esports), an Elo-style iRating sorts drivers into sessions and divisions, and 13-week seasons rotate tracks weekly. Skill rating and matchmaking have no mechanic in the taxonomy (proposed as skill-rating-matchmaking).

name: Islanders
summary: A minimalist placement puzzle in which every building scores points from compatible and incompatible neighbors on a procedural island, and score thresholds unlock new building packs and new islands.
core_loop: choose a building from the inventory -> preview its point value from neighbors and terrain -> place it permanently -> score thresholds restock and offer a choice of two packs -> fill the gauge to move to a new island
design_notes: Islanders reduces the city builder to its placement rule: no resources, traffic, citizens, or research, only point values from proximity to compatible structures and natural features and penalties for incompatible ones. Placements are permanent, so each choice consumes space, and the run ends when buildings or space run out before the next threshold. It is included as a boundary case for adjacency scoring, since nothing in the world evolves without the player.

name: Job Simulator
summary: A room-scale VR comedy set in a museum run by robots, where the player performs parodied office, kitchen, store, and garage tasks by grabbing and manipulating physics objects.
core_loop: job bot gives a task -> grab and manipulate objects with tracked hands -> appliances and props react physically -> task completes -> next task until the job ends
design_notes: Included as a boundary case for its interaction model: nearly every object within reach is a physics object that can be picked up, thrown, or combined, and fixed appliances expose buttons, levers, and dials. Tasks are authored and loose, so variety comes from physical improvisation such as choosing pizza toppings or tire styles rather than from a modeled occupation. After all four jobs, modifiers alter the physics.

name: Jurassic World Evolution
summary: A dinosaur park management game in which the player excavates fossils for DNA, breeds and modifies dinosaurs, and keeps them contained through storms, sabotage, and breakouts while balancing three division contracts.
core_loop: send expeditions for fossils -> sequence DNA and modify genomes -> incubate dinosaurs -> meet feeding and social needs in enclosures -> guests spend while divisions offer contracts -> contain storms and breakouts -> raise the star rating to unlock islands
design_notes: Jurassic World Evolution turns a park sim into a containment problem. Each species has feeding, social, and territory needs; unmet needs lower comfort, and low-comfort dinosaurs fight, break fences, and escape to attack guests. Three divisions (Science, Security, Entertainment) offer contracts and track reputation, and letting one fall triggers sabotage such as a power shutdown or disease outbreak, which turns faction standing into a source of hazards. Genome modification changes a species' stats, aggression, and appearance, and the player can drive ranger and ACU vehicles to sedate, medicate, transport, and repair. Dinosaurs do not breed in this game; adding modern-species DNA to a genome trades stats against aggression, a rule the taxonomy lacks (proposed as genome-modification).

name: Kenshi
summary: A squad-based open-world RPG with no hero character, where any recruit can starve, lose limbs, train skills by doing, be enslaved, or found an outpost among reactive factions.
core_loop: wander the world with a squad -> fight, trade, steal, or get captured -> injuries and hunger reduce stats while skills train from use -> recruit and found an outpost -> factions react and world states shift
design_notes: There is no main character: every recruit and NPC is a potential equal, with no hero units given stronger stats, and the world and shops do not scale to the player, so early characters are weaker than most people they meet. Progress comes from use-based skill gain, which makes losing fights a form of training. Deaths of notable faction leaders change world states, such as towns taken over by a new faction. Chris Hunt developed it alone until 2013, and it was one of the first games in Steam Early Access.

name: Kerbal Space Program
summary: A space flight sim where the player assembles rockets from parts and flies them under patched-conic orbital physics and atmospheric aerodynamics through a scaled-down planetary system.
core_loop: assemble a craft from parts -> launch and stage through the atmosphere -> plan maneuver nodes and burn for orbit or transfer -> land, dock, or crash -> return science, funds, and reputation -> unlock parts and design a more ambitious craft
design_notes: Stock orbits use a patched-conic approximation: a vessel is attracted by one body at a time and switches at sphere-of-influence boundaries, so there are no Lagrange points, but coasting vessels can be propagated on rails during time warp. Vessels are trees of parts joined by joints of limited strength, so mass distribution, thrust placement, and staging order decide whether a design flies, wobbles, or tears apart. Failure (stranded or dead Kerbals, debris) is a source of player stories rather than a hard stop, and Career mode layers funds, reputation, and contracts on top of the physics sandbox.

name: Kingdoms and Castles
summary: A medieval town builder in which peasants farm and stockpile for an annual winter while the player stacks castle blocks into walls and towers to defend against vikings, dragons, and ogres.
core_loop: place a keep and houses on an island -> peasants farm, cut wood, and quarry -> store food for the annual winter -> tax peasants to pay workers and unlock buildings -> stack castle blocks into walls and towers -> repel vikings, dragons, and ogres
design_notes: Kingdoms and Castles pairs a light town economy with a block-built castle: walls and towers form from how blocks are stacked, and taller archer towers reach farther, so defense is shaped geometry rather than a building menu. Each villager and resource is individually simulated, and an annual winter that destroys crops sets a regular survival check. Raiders kidnap peasants and burn buildings, and a dragon targets granaries, linking defense to food security.

name: Lemonade Stand
summary: A 1973 educational business sim in which the player runs a lemonade stand for 12 days, setting glasses made, advertising signs, and price against a daily weather report.
core_loop: read the weather report -> choose glasses to make, signs to buy, and price per glass -> demand resolves into sales -> profit or a storm loss -> reinvest the next day
design_notes: Lemonade Stand reduces a business to three daily inputs (glasses made, advertising signs, price per glass) and one exogenous variable, the weather (sunny, cloudy, or hot and dry), which shifts demand. Shocks are random: thunderstorms on cloudy days wipe out the day's investment, and street closures or wind that blows signs away also occur. Up to 30 players can each run an independent stand under the same weather. Signs are an early case of advertising spend used as a demand lever; the taxonomy has no mechanic for marketing spend, so the run proposes advertising-awareness.

name: Little Computer People
summary: A 1985 home-computer life sim in which one procedurally seeded little person lives in a cross-section of a three-story house, follows a daily routine, and depends on the player for food, water, and attention.
core_loop: watch the resident's routine -> hunger, thirst, and mood drift -> deliver food, water, gifts, or pats -> type polite requests -> mood decides whether he complies -> repeat across sessions
