design_notes: Rich Gold conceived the game and David Crane built it at Activision; the documentation presents the little people as real beings living inside the computer, with the player as their caretaker. Each disk's serial number seeded the resident's name (from 256), shirt color, personality, and behavior, so every copy hosted a different person. There is no win condition: the resident cooks, reads, plays piano, phones, and types letters about his feelings on a day of about six real-time hours, and his mood gates whether typed requests are obeyed. The cassette C64 version dropped memory, letters, and card games, which shows which systems carried the sense of a persistent person.

name: Manor Lords
summary: An early-access medieval city builder in which families settle gridless burgage plots along curved roads, fields depend on soil fertility and crop rotation, and the lord fields retinue and militia in real-time battles.
core_loop: draw curved roads and burgage plots -> families move in and staff workplaces -> fields, backyard extensions, and production chains feed the market -> taxes, tithes, and trade fund a retinue -> defend against bandits and rival lords
design_notes: Manor Lords drops the zoning grid: the player draws plots against freely curved roads, the game divides them into burgage plots, and households extend them with backyard gardens, chickens, or goats, so housing is also production. Fields carry soil fertility per crop that rotation preserves, and hunting depends on animal populations that overexpansion drives away. Militia levies come from the town's own families, so each battle death is a lost worker; the game remained in early access as of August 2026.

name: Microsoft Flight Simulator (2020)
summary: A flight sim that streams a photorealistic model of the whole Earth built from map and photogrammetry data and flies aircraft through live weather with a surface-level aerodynamic model.
core_loop: pick aircraft, airport, and time -> preflight and start up -> take off into live or set weather -> navigate and hand-fly or use autopilot -> approach and land -> pick the next flight
design_notes: The world is data rather than authored terrain: Bing Maps imagery refreshed every 28 days, Blackshark.ai photogrammetry, and Azure AI 3D generation streamed from more than two petabytes, with Meteoblue weather and real air traffic fed in live. The flight model simulates over 1,000 control surfaces and wind over terrain, and a legacy model is kept as an option. No mechanic in the taxonomy covers simulation state driven by real-world data feeds (proposed as real-world-data-feeds).

name: Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024
summary: The successor to Microsoft Flight Simulator (2020) that adds a career mode of certified aviation jobs, walk-around preflight, revised aircraft systems, and modeled ground surfaces to the streamed whole-Earth flight sim.
core_loop: choose a career job -> walk around the aircraft for preflight -> start systems -> fly the mission profile (firefighting, rescue, cargo hook, airline) -> earn experience, reputation, and certifications -> unlock specializations
design_notes: Career mode turns the 2020 sandbox into a progression game: aerial firefighting, search and rescue, crop dusting, helicopter cargo hook, outsize cargo in the Airbus Beluga, arctic cargo in the A400M, and airline flights are gated by certifications and specializations earned through experience and reputation. Aircraft physics and systems (electrical, fuel, pneumatic, hydraulic) were revised, and stones, gravel, and grass are modeled in 3D and affect wheels. The launch showed the cost of a streamed world: an overwhelmed database cache caused long loads and missing content.

name: Mindustry
summary: An open-source automation tower defense game in which the player belts ore into factories that supply turrets, units, and the core against enemy waves while capturing campaign sectors on two planets, with an assembly-like logic language for controlling blocks and units.
core_loop: drill ore -> belt items to the core and factories -> build and supply turrets -> survive scheduled enemy waves -> research new blocks with core resources -> capture sectors and launch resources between them
design_notes: Mindustry began as a 2017 itch.io jam game and fuses Factorio-style belt logistics with tower defense: turrets consume belted ammunition, power, and coolant, so the factory's layout is the defense, and survival maps send progressively stronger waves at the core on a timer. Version 6 (2020) added RTS units built in factories and upgraded through reconstructors, and Mindustry Logic, an assembly-like language that runs on processor blocks, reads sensors and memory cells, and can bind and command units. The campaign spans Serpulo and Erekir with 35 hand-made maps and 250+ procedural sectors whose production continues while the player is elsewhere and is moved between sectors by launch pads. The game is GPL-3.0 and free from the author while also sold on Steam, so community servers, plugins, and mods are unrestricted.

name: Minecraft
summary: A procedurally generated voxel sandbox where players mine blocks, craft tools, survive hostile night mobs and hunger, farm and trade, and build circuits from redstone.
core_loop: explore a generated world -> mine blocks and gather resources -> craft tools, armor, and workstations -> build shelter before night mobs spawn -> farm, breed, and trade -> dig deeper or travel to the Nether and End for rarer materials
design_notes: The world is an effectively infinite grid of one-meter blocks generated from a seed with biomes, caves, and ore distributions, and every block can be removed or placed, so terrain is both resource and building material. Survival pressure is light (hunger, health, light-level mob spawning on a 20-minute day cycle) and leaves room for self-set goals. Redstone gives the block world wires, power sources, repeaters, and pistons, which players use to build farms, logic gates, and working computers. The game began as a public alpha in May 2009 and reached 1.0 in November 2011.

name: Mini Metro
summary: A minimalist subway-design game where the player draws and redraws lines between shape-coded stations under a weekly ration of trains and tunnels until a station overcrowds.
core_loop: new stations appear -> draw or reroute lines -> trains carry shape-matched passengers -> weekly grant of new assets -> demand outgrows capacity -> a station overcrowds and the run ends
design_notes: Mini Metro abstracts a metro network into station shapes, passengers drawn as the shape of the station type they want to reach, and a scarce inventory of lines, locomotives, tunnels, and bridges. New stations keep appearing while supply arrives only as a weekly grant, so the player keeps redrawing a network that is always under capacity. Failure is local and visible: a station over its limit (typically six passengers) for long enough ends the run. Modes vary the rules: Extreme fixes lines once placed, Endless removes overcrowding, and Creative is a sandbox.

name: Motorsport Manager
summary: A racing team management game in which the player designs car parts across seasons, hires drivers and staff, and makes live strategy calls on tyres, pit stops, and weather while races are simulated.
core_loop: design and build car parts -> hire drivers, designers, and mechanics -> set race weekend strategy -> race simulates with tyre, fuel, and weather calls -> results earn money and standing -> develop next season's car
design_notes: Motorsport Manager splits the job into a between-races engineering game and a live race game. Between races the player commissions car parts and chooses which go into next season's car, trading performance against development time. During races the simulation runs in real time with pause, and the player decides tyre compounds, pit timing, and whether to gamble on a fast pit stop or stay on slicks as dynamic weather changes. Drivers have personality types that cause team drama and respond to tough love or support. A simpler mobile game of the same name was released on iOS in 2014; this entry covers the 2016 PC game.

name: M.U.L.E.
summary: A four-player economic strategy game on a colony planet where players outfit M.U.L.E. robots to produce food, energy, smithore, and crystite and trade them in real-time auctions.
core_loop: claim a land grant -> buy and outfit M.U.L.E.s and walk them to plots -> production with shortages and random events -> real-time auctions set prices -> buy or sell -> next round
design_notes: M.U.L.E. couples its four resources: food sets how long a player's development turn lasts, energy shortages stop plots from producing, and smithore supply sets M.U.L.E. prices and whether the store can manufacture more. Prices are set in real-time auctions in which buyers and sellers move avatars toward a price, so withholding goods and private deals between players are legitimate tactics. Danielle Bunten built catch-up rules into the systems: tied bids go to the player in the losing position, favorable events rarely hit the leader and harmful ones never hit last place, and land auctions were replaced by free grants because they compounded the leader's advantage. The taxonomy has no mechanic for systematic catch-up rules (proposed as catch-up-balancing).

name: Nintendogs
summary: A Nintendo DS puppy sim in which the player pets, washes, feeds, and walks up to three dogs, teaches them tricks with recorded voice commands, and enters disc, agility, and obedience trials.
core_loop: care for the dog by touch -> teach tricks by voice -> walk the dog and find items -> enter disc, agility, and obedience trials -> earn prize money and trainer points -> buy supplies and unlock new breeds
design_notes: Nintendogs was built to show off DS hardware: the touchscreen handles petting, grooming, and washing, and the microphone handles the dog's name and trick commands. Care runs on the DS clock, so hunger, thirst, and coat condition worsen with elapsed time, but dogs cannot die, breed, or age, which makes neglect a recoverable setback rather than a fail state. Trials have five classes from Beginner to Championship, and placing third or better promotes a dog. Bark Mode lets nearby players' dogs meet and exchange presents.

name: Noita
summary: A roguelite action game in which every pixel of the world is simulated as a falling-sand material that burns, melts, flows, and reacts, and the player builds wands from spells to dig through procedurally generated levels.
core_loop: descend into a procedurally generated biome -> fight enemies with wands that also reshape the pixel world -> survive fire, liquids, and gases set off by fighting -> buy or find spells and rebuild wands at the Holy Mountain -> descend again or die and restart
design_notes: Noita's Falling Everything engine simulates each pixel as a material with state (solid, powder, liquid, gas) and reaction rules, and solid bodies are Box2D rigid bodies that break into pixels when damaged. Because spells, enemies, and the player all act on that layer, combat routinely sets off chain events such as burning oil, steam explosions, flooding, and collapsing ceilings, and these kill the player as often as enemies do. Wand building composes spells with modifiers into programs with cast order and mana limits, and runs are permadeath.

name: Offworld Trading Company
summary: A real-time economic strategy game on Mars where companies claim resource tiles, refine goods for a shared market whose prices move with every trade, and win by buying out every rival's stock.
core_loop: land an HQ -> claim tiles and build extractors -> refine resources into goods -> sell into a market whose prices move with each trade -> buy black market sabotage and stock -> buy out every rival
design_notes: Soren Johnson replaced combat with a shared market: 13 resources trade at prices that move with every purchase and sale, so selling a large stockpile drives the price down and one player's bulk purchases create openings for others. Black market items such as nukes, EMPs, and mutinies act through the economy, and each purchase raises the price of the next one. Victory comes from equity: players buy shares in rivals until they hold a majority of every company, and buying back one's own shares makes a takeover more expensive. Johnson names M.U.L.E. and Railroad Tycoon as inspirations.

name: Opus Magnum
summary: A programming puzzle game in which the player builds alchemical machines from arms, tracks, and glyphs on a hex grid, programs them on an instruction timeline, and compares each looping solution's cost, cycles, and area against other players' histograms.
core_loop: read the reagents and product -> place arms, tracks, and glyphs on the hex grid -> write instructions on the timeline -> run until the required products are made -> compare cost, cycles, and area histograms -> export a looping GIF or optimize
design_notes: Opus Magnum refines Zach Barth's 2008 Flash game The Codex of Alchemical Engineering into Zachtronics' most permissive puzzle design: there is no part limit, any machine that delivers the products counts, and the difficulty is choosing among three competing metrics. Arms grab, rotate, pivot, extend, and move on tracks under a per-arm instruction tape, and glyphs bond, unbond, calcify, and project metals one step toward gold. Solutions are ranked on cost in gold, cycles, and area, with no in-game reward for optimizing, so motivation comes from friends' scores and the histograms. Barth's experience with solution recording in Infinifactory led to built-in export of seamlessly looping GIFs, which made solutions shareable outside the game; a puzzle editor feeds Steam Workshop.

name: The Oregon Trail
summary: An educational turn-based travel sim in which the player buys supplies and sets rations for a wagon journey to Oregon while random events, weather, and illness threaten the party.
developer: Don Rawitsch, Bill Heinemann, and Paul Dillenberger; later MECC
core_loop: buy supplies at the outset and at forts -> choose food consumption and pace each leg -> random events, weather, and illness hit the party -> hunt for food and cross rivers -> reach Oregon or die on the trail
design_notes: Three student teachers wrote it in two weeks for a Minneapolis classroom, where it debuted on 3 December 1971; MECC distributed it on its time-sharing network from 1975 and on the Apple II from 1980. The 1971 model is a few stocks (food, bullets, clothing, supplies, cash) spent over about twelve two-week rounds, with one or two random events and weather drawn each round and typed hunting that rewards speed. The 1985 graphical version added adjustable pace and rations, river crossings by fording, caulking, or ferry, a party of five, professions that set difficulty and score, and tombstones left by earlier players.

name: Out of the Park Baseball
summary: A text-based baseball management sim in which the player runs a franchise's roster, scouting, draft, trades, and finances while a pitch-by-pitch engine simulates games for career, historical, or fictional leagues.
core_loop: scout and draft players -> set rosters, lineups, and depth charts -> simulate games pitch by pitch -> players develop or decline -> trade, sign, and manage finances -> build a franchise across seasons
design_notes: OOTP simulates baseball pitch by pitch from player ratings and reports it as scrolling play-by-play text with a minimal diamond, plus 3D ballparks and ball flight from OOTP 15. Its range of setups defines it: real current leagues under the MLB and Minor League Baseball licenses from OOTP 16, historical play that drops the player into any era with real rookies arriving each season, and fictional leagues. Ratings are filtered through scouting, so the GM sees estimates rather than true values. The league keeps a full statistical history with HTML reports, so long careers build an almanac.

name: Oxygen Not Included
summary: A side-view colony sim in which a few duplicants survive inside an asteroid where every tile holds an element with mass and temperature, so air, liquids, heat, and germs flow through the base.
core_loop: dig into the asteroid -> lay out rooms, pipes, and wires -> duplicants perform prioritized errands -> oxygen, heat, germs, and waste redistribute tile by tile -> stress and shortfalls surface -> rebuild toward closed, sustainable loops
design_notes: Each cell holds one element with a mass and a temperature, and heat moves between cells every 0.2 s tick by conduction, so insulation, phase changes, and overheating machines follow from one rule rather than from per-building scripts. Most machines emit byproducts (a natural gas generator makes 800 W plus polluted water and carbon dioxide), so the long game is closing loops so waste becomes input. Mood uses a morale-versus-expectation gap: learning skills raises a duplicant's expectation, so better-trained colonists need better food, rooms, and decor. Wikipedia names Dwarf Fortress, Prison Architect, and The Sims as design influences.

name: Papers, Please
summary: A border inspection game in which the player checks entrants' documents against daily-changing rules on a timed shift and spends the wages on a family's rent, food, and heat.
core_loop: read the day's rules -> inspect each entrant's papers -> interrogate, fingerprint, or scan discrepancies -> stamp approve, deny, or detain -> citations and bribes adjust pay -> pay rent, food, and heat -> next day adds rules
design_notes: The inspection rules are predicates that accumulate day by day as the fictional state's politics shift, so the same entrant generator yields harder cases over time. Pay is per correctly processed entrant within a fixed shift and citations arrive by fax after each error, which makes speed and accuracy a direct trade. The household ledger converts that trade into moral pressure, and bribes and rule-bending choices feed scripted branches that lead to twenty endings.

name: Paralives
summary: An indie life sim, in early access since May 2026, in which players build grid-less homes and guide Parafolks with needs, emotions, traits, skills, and careers in an open-world town.
core_loop: design Parafolks in the Paramaker -> build a grid-less home -> Parafolks pursue needs and wants -> socialize, work, and build skills around town -> relationships, children, and aging change the household -> share homes and Parafolks on the Workshop
design_notes: Paralives began as Alex Massé's solo project, was funded through Patreon (over 15,000 supporters by November 2023), and entered Steam early access on 2026-05-25 with about two years planned before 1.0. Its building tools are its most distinctive system: walls and furniture resize, recolor, and stack, walls can curve, floors can split level, and a road-style wall tool was inspired by Cities: Skylines. Conversation fills a together bar that unlocks together cards, multiselect lets several Parafolks act as a group, and procedural animation adapts to preceding animations.

name: PC Building Simulator
summary: A workshop sim in which the player takes email jobs to build, upgrade, repair, and overclock PCs from licensed parts and verifies the results with benchmark software.
developer: Claudiu Kiss and The Irregular Corporation
core_loop: accept an email job -> order parts with a shipping tier -> open the case and diagnose or assemble -> install software, remove viruses, or overclock -> benchmark -> get paid -> pay rent and electricity -> unlock better parts
design_notes: Parts are licensed real components with compatibility rules, and a machine's performance is measured with the real 3DMark benchmark, so a build's quality is an output of its parts rather than a designer-set score. Assembly has physical consequences: a CPU cooler mounted without thermal paste lets the processor overheat and fail. The career wraps this in a small business with monthly rent and electricity, accept-or-reject email jobs, and timed jobs that become more common later.

name: Pharaoh
summary: An Egyptian city builder on the Caesar III engine in which a yearly Nile flood waters floodplain farms, walkers carry services to housing, five gods must be appeased, and monuments take years of labor and materials.
core_loop: lay out housing, roads, and floodplain farms -> the yearly Nile flood waters the farms -> walkers deliver services, food, and goods to houses -> houses evolve and pay taxes -> appease five gods and build monuments to meet mission goals
design_notes: Pharaoh reuses Caesar III's walker model and adds a calendar driven by the Nile: floodplain farms can only be worked between floods, irrigation ditches raise fertility, and the god Osiris can improve or worsen the flood. Monuments need worker facilities and delivered materials and take in-game years, a construction-logistics system with no exact taxonomy match (see run proposal). Five gods (Ra, Bast, Osiris, Ptah, Seth) grant gifts when appeased with shrines and temples and send disasters when angered.

name: Plague Inc.
summary: A strategy game in which the player evolves a pathogen's transmission, symptoms, and abilities to infect and kill the world's population before humanity's cure research finishes.
core_loop: infect patient zero -> infections spread within and between countries -> earn DNA points -> buy transmission, symptom, and ability evolutions -> severity raises awareness and cure funding -> race to kill everyone before the cure completes
design_notes: James Vaughan's game inverts the epidemic model: the player owns the pathogen's parameters, and humanity's response (awareness, closures, cure research) is the opponent. The tension is between infectivity and severity, because visible symptoms and deaths accelerate the cure, so successful plans spread quietly and then turn lethal. Countries differ by climate and conditions the pathogen must adapt to, and the CDC invited Vaughan to discuss its infection model in 2013, though Ndemic has said it is not on par with scientific models. Evolved adds 10 disease types, 23 scenarios, versus and co-op modes, and a scenario creator with Workshop sharing.

name: Planet Coaster
summary: A 3D theme park builder with a spline and piece coaster editor, modular scenery, and individually simulated guests and staff, built around sharing creations through the Steam Workshop.
core_loop: sculpt terrain and build modular scenery -> design coasters and test their ratings -> guests choose rides, shops, and paths -> manage staff, prices, and finances -> share parks and blueprints on the Workshop
design_notes: Planet Coaster keeps the RollerCoaster Tycoon structure of rated rides and guests with preferences and moves the emphasis to construction: a hybrid spline and piece coaster editor, a voxel terrain editor, and modular pieces that snap into custom buildings. The Workshop is part of play, since players import coasters, scenery blueprints, and whole parks made by others. Frontier calls it a spiritual successor to its own RollerCoaster Tycoon 3, and both run on Frontier's Cobra engine. Career, Challenge (limited funds and research), and Sandbox (unlimited funds) modes share one simulation.

name: Planet Zoo
summary: A zoo management game where the player builds habitats to meet each species' welfare needs, manages genetics and breeding, and raises a conservation rating, using Planet Coaster's building tools.
core_loop: build a habitat for a species' needs -> animals respond to space, terrain, enrichment, and group size -> breed and manage genomes -> trade or release animals for conservation -> guests pay and learn -> expand the zoo
design_notes: Planet Zoo gives each animal species a requirements profile (habitat size, land and water, terrain and plant biome, temperature, group size and sex ratio, enrichment, privacy, and guest exposure) and reports the shortfalls as welfare, so habitat design is a constraint-satisfaction problem. Each animal carries a genome that affects lifespan, size, health, and fertility; offspring inherit it, and inbreeding harms the young, which turns breeding into a population-genetics task. Franchise mode connects zoos to an online market where players buy and trade animals with conservation credits. It reuses Planet Coaster's construction and Workshop tools.

name: Poly Bridge
summary: A bridge-building puzzle game where the player places beams and roads from materials with different costs and strengths under a budget, then runs a physics test as vehicles cross.
core_loop: read anchors, vehicles, and budget -> place beams and roads from materials -> run the simulation -> watch stress and failures -> trim cost or reinforce -> submit to leaderboard
design_notes: Bridges are trusses of joints and members in a side-view plane; each material (road, wood, steel, rope, cable, hydraulics) has its own cost, strength, and mass, and crossing vehicles load the structure until members exceed their limit and snap. The puzzle is minimizing cost under a level budget while keeping stress below breaking, and hydraulic phases tied to vehicle checkpoints let bridges move in sync with traffic. Failed runs are free to repeat, so the loop is fast iteration against a stress readout.

name: Populous
summary: The first god game, in which the player raises and lowers land so followers can build and multiply, then spends the mana they generate on disasters against a rival deity's people.
core_loop: raise and lower land to make flat ground -> followers settle and build houses -> houses breed followers and raise mana -> spend mana on knights, earthquakes, swamps, volcanoes, and floods -> overwhelm the rival deity's followers
design_notes: Populous established the god game by making terrain the player's main tool and population the player's currency: flat land lets followers build larger houses, houses produce followers, and followers produce mana for powers, so shaping the land is also running the economy. The landscape type of each world (desert, lava, snow and ice) changes how followers develop. Population growth from housing has no mechanic id yet (proposal filed). The game ships 500 worlds, each won by outgrowing and destroying the opposing population.

name: PowerWash Simulator
summary: A first-person cleaning sim in which the player power-washes vehicles and buildings, choosing nozzles and soaps to strip dirt layers until every part reports clean.
core_loop: accept a job -> pick nozzle and soap -> wash surfaces -> per-part progress reaches 100 percent -> job pays -> buy washer upgrades -> next job
design_notes: The simulation is a per-surface dirt state: each surface carries layers (dirt, grime, lichen, moss, rust) that the spray removes according to nozzle, soap, and range, and every object reports its percentage done. Four nozzles trade power against spray width, so play is matching the tool to the layer and distance. Progress bars per object and a highlight for remaining dirt make completion fully legible, and the career's story arrives as client text messages rather than through the simulation.

name: Princess Maker 2
summary: A raising sim in which the player, as a father figure, schedules a daughter's training, part-time jobs, rest, and adventures from age 10 to 18, and her accumulated attributes decide one of 74 endings.
core_loop: set three activity periods for the month -> training and jobs change attributes, money, and fatigue -> events and festivals test her attributes -> rest or vacation to prevent illness -> she ages a year -> at 18 her attributes select a career ending
design_notes: Takami Akai designed the sequel to answer complaints that the original was repetitive, adding more reactions and events around a schedule-and-attributes core. Each month splits into early, middle, and late periods, each assigned to training (academic, artistic, religious, military, or magical), a part-time job, adventure, or free time, under a small annual income. Jobs unlock with age and pay promotion and streak bonuses, rival girls age alongside the daughter as benchmarks, and October festivals hold contests in martial arts, dance, art, and cooking. At 18 her attributes and history select one of 74 career endings, a branching-outcome model captured by the care-dependent-development mechanic.

name: Prison Architect
summary: A prison management sim in which the player builds a facility, sets an hourly regime, and staffs it while hundreds of prisoners pursue needs whose neglect leads to fights, escapes, and riots.
core_loop: build cells, canteens, and yards -> set the hourly regime -> prisoners pursue needs within the schedule -> unmet needs raise misconduct, contraband, and riots -> hire staff, run programs, and claim grants -> expand capacity for more prisoners and income
design_notes: Control is indirect: the player cannot order prisoners, only shape the regime, the buildings that satisfy each need, and the staff who enforce rules. Each of about 21 needs is a charge from 1 to 10 satisfied by specific objects for set durations (a phone booth takes 25 minutes, a shower 20), and needs left at the top charge produce side effects. Information itself is a staffed system: features such as viewing finances unlock only after hiring the matching staff member, such as an accountant. Prisoners fall into five security levels with different temperaments, sentence lengths, and cashflow, and reform and labor programs reduce recidivism, which feeds the prison's grade.

name: Project Hospital
summary: A hospital management sim in which the player builds departments and hires staff while doctors diagnose patients by ordering examinations that reveal symptoms until one diagnosis remains.
core_loop: sign insurer contracts -> patients arrive with complaints -> doctors order examinations and lab tests -> revealed symptoms narrow the diagnosis -> treat, hospitalize, or operate -> insurers pay -> build departments and hire staff
design_notes: Oxymoron Games reduced medicine to symptom rules: each diagnosis has symptoms with tuned occurrence frequencies, examinations reveal them, and a diagnosis becomes clear once enough are found; frequencies were set so a case is rarely obvious after the first exam. Patients reach the hospital through insurance company contracts, and the developers say the resulting economy came to resemble the American system. The free Doctor Mode update lets the player make individual doctors' exam and treatment choices, turning the facility sim into a diagnosis game.

name: Project Sid
summary: An Altera research demonstration that runs 10 to 1,000-plus language-model agents with the concurrent PIANO architecture in Minecraft to study role specialization, collective rule-making, and cultural transmission.
core_loop: seed agents with personas and community goals -> concurrent modules perceive, remember, talk, and act in Minecraft -> cognitive controller commits a coherent decision -> roles specialize and rules are paid, debated, and amended -> beliefs and memes spread between towns
design_notes: PIANO runs about ten modules concurrently at different speeds (memory, action awareness, goal generation, social awareness, talking, skill execution), with fast non-language reflex networks and a cognitive controller that acts as a bottleneck and broadcasts one decision so speech and action stay consistent; GPT-4o was the strongest base model. In 30-agent runs agents settled into persistent roles (farmer, miner, engineer, guard, explorer, blacksmith) that collapsed without the social module. In a 29-agent constitution experiment with a 20 percent tax paid into community chests every 120 seconds, pro- and anti-tax influencers shifted votes, amendments passed, and payments followed the new rate. In a 500-agent run, Pastafarianism seeded by 20 priests spread to other towns; 1,000-agent attempts exceeded the Minecraft server's capacity. The preprint states no public code release.

name: Project Zomboid
summary: An isometric zombie survival sandbox in which one survivor manages moodles, injuries, skills, and failing utilities across a large Kentucky map until an inevitable death.
core_loop: loot houses and stores -> avoid or fight zombies drawn by sight and noise -> manage hunger, fatigue, injuries, and moodles -> utilities fail and seasons turn -> barricade, farm, and level skills -> survive until death
design_notes: The framing question is how the character dies, not whether: zombie infection is always fatal in an unmodified game, so play is about extending a doomed run. Water and power shut off within the first month, after which erosion and overgrowth spread, giving the sandbox a scheduled decline. Zombies respond to sight and hearing and hordes migrate, so noise from actions shapes risk; there is no mechanic id for noise attraction yet (proposal filed). The game has been in early access since a paid tech demo in May 2011, with Steam early access from November 2013 and Build 42 in open beta from December 2024.

name: Prom Week
summary: A 2012 browser social sim in which the player picks social exchanges among 18 high school students in the week before prom, with the Comme il Faut rule system deciding who wants to do what and how targets respond.
developer: UC Santa Cruz Expressive Intelligence Studio
core_loop: pick a level goal -> choose an initiator, a target, and a social exchange -> rules score volition and acceptance -> relationships, statuses, and history update -> new exchanges open -> the goal is met or the story turns another way
design_notes: Prom Week runs on Comme il Faut (CiF), which its UCSC authors describe as making social relationships playable: characters have traits, interests, statuses, and directed networks of liking, attraction, and respect, and more than 5,000 social considerations govern what each character wants and how others respond. The player never writes dialogue but chooses which social exchange a character initiates; CiF offers the exchanges a character is inclined toward, ranked by likelihood, and resolves acceptance from the social state of everyone involved, including what third parties think. Levels set story goals such as getting two characters to date, which turns the rule base into a puzzle with many solutions.

name: Railroad Tycoon
summary: A railroad business sim in which the player lays track, builds stations, schedules trains to meet regional supply and demand, and battles rival barons through the stock market.
core_loop: lay track and place stations -> buy trains and set consists and stops -> carry cargo to stations where it is demanded -> revenue and industry growth -> raise capital through bonds and stock -> defend against rival barons
design_notes: Railroad Tycoon joins a train-operations model to a corporate-finance model. Stations come in four sizes (signal tower, depot, station, terminal) with growing service areas, and an economy setting chooses between a simple economy where big cities buy almost anything and a complex one where they buy only certain goods. The company starts with $1 million split between equity and a loan, raises more through bonds, and trades in a small stock market where rival barons attempt buyouts and rate wars. Meier took the idea from the board game 1830 and also cited SimCity. Track construction has no matching mechanic in the taxonomy (proposed as track-laying), and dated vehicle availability is proposed as dated-tech-timeline.

name: Rebel Inc.
summary: A counterinsurgency strategy game in which the player, as a coalition governor, spends a monthly budget on civilian and military initiatives to build popular support and stabilize regions of a war-torn country while corruption, inflation, and an insurgency push back.
core_loop: fund civilian initiatives in regions -> popular support rises -> spending raises corruption and inflation -> an insurgency emerges and contests regions -> deploy troops, counter corruption, or negotiate -> stabilize the country to win
design_notes: Rebel Inc. inverts Ndemic's earlier Plague Inc.: instead of spreading a disease, the player contains an insurgency by building popular support, and spending itself generates corruption and inflation. The tension is between civilian initiatives that win support slowly and military spending that holds ground without building support. Corruption as a side effect of spending is not yet a mechanic in the taxonomy (proposal corruption-leakage).

name: Reigns
summary: A swipe-based card game in which the player, as a succession of medieval monarchs, accepts or rejects advisers' requests that push church, people, army, and treasury meters, and each reign ends when any meter empties or fills.
core_loop: draw an adviser's card -> swipe left or right -> church, people, army, and treasury meters shift -> a meter hits empty or full -> the king dies -> the next reign begins with unlocked cards
design_notes: Reigns reduces governance to four bounded meters in which both extremes are fatal, so every choice is a balancing act rather than a maximization. The swipe interface, modeled on Tinder, keeps each decision binary and fast. It is a boundary case included for the dilemma-card mechanic and its use of death as progress between reigns.

name: RimWorld
summary: A colony sim where a few named colonists with needs, traits, injuries, and relationships survive on a frontier planet while a storyteller AI paces events.
core_loop: designate work -> colonists self-assign by priority -> needs and moods shift -> storyteller injects events -> colony adapts or collapses
design_notes: Tynan Sylvester describes RimWorld as a story generator. Its systems are chosen for how legible and story-relevant their outputs are rather than for realism: thoughts are itemized with sources and durations, injuries are named body parts, and raids scale with colony wealth to keep tension.

name: RollerCoaster Tycoon
summary: An amusement park management game in which the player builds rides and custom coasters piece by piece, rated for excitement, intensity, and nausea, to satisfy guests with individual preferences and meet scenario goals.
core_loop: build paths, rides, and shops -> design coasters and test their ratings -> guests choose rides by intensity preference and budget -> thoughts reveal problems -> adjust prices, staff, and layout -> meet the scenario goal
design_notes: RollerCoaster Tycoon makes ride design measurable: every built ride is test-run and rated on excitement, intensity, and nausea, and each guest has a preferred intensity and a nausea tolerance, so the ratings decide who will ride and who gets sick afterward. Guests are individual agents with money, needs, and a stream of readable thoughts, which makes park problems inspectable one guest at a time. Rides lose reliability with age and break down unless mechanics inspect them on a player-set interval. Scenario goals (guest counts and park rating by a deadline) chain 21 base parks. OpenRCT2, a reimplementation of RCT2, carries the systems forward, and Planet Coaster and Parkitect are described as spiritual successors.

name: Satisfactory
summary: A first-person 3D factory automation game in which a pioneer taps infinite resource nodes on an alien planet and connects machines with belts, pipes, trains, and drones to deliver project parts to FICSIT's Space Elevator.
core_loop: scout resource nodes -> place miners -> belt ore through smelters, constructors, and assemblers -> deliver parts to the HUB and Space Elevator -> unlock the next tier -> expand power and logistics to distant nodes
design_notes: Satisfactory moves the Factorio-style ratio puzzle into a hand-built 3D world explored on foot, so verticality, foundations, and architecture become part of layout and many players build for appearance as well as throughput. Resource nodes never deplete and are graded impure, normal, or pure (0.5x, 1x, 2x), so expansion is driven by needing more node types and output rather than by exhaustion. The power grid fails as a whole: when demand exceeds supply and storage is empty the fuse trips and every connected building stops until the player resets it, unlike grids that slow machines proportionally. Clock speed (1% to 250%, with Power Shards and a power exponent of about 1.32) and 106 alternate recipes from crash-site hard drives give each factory a recipe-selection layer that the taxonomy folds into production-chain; this run proposed a machine-boosting mechanic for clock speed and similar systems, and a megaproject-sink mechanic for the Space Elevator. There are no base-raiding enemies; fauna threaten only the pioneer.

name: Schedule I
summary: A first-person crime business sim in which the player grows and cooks drugs, mixes ingredients to create products with effects customers want, sells them around a city under police pressure, and automates production with hired staff.
core_loop: grow or cook a base product -> mix in ingredients to add effects -> sell to customers who want those effects -> avoid police searches and curfews -> hire dealers and staff -> buy properties -> unlock new regions
design_notes: Schedule I runs a production business through a first-person avatar: the player waters plants, operates mixing and cooking stations, and walks or drives deals across Hyland Point before hiring dealers, botanists, cooks, and janitors to automate the chain. Mixing common ingredients such as soft drinks or paracetamol into a product adds effects that raise its sale value, and customers want particular effects, so recipe discovery is the product-development layer. Police pressure rises with growth through random searches, roadblocks, and curfews, and being seen breaking the law sets a wanted status, a player-heat rule the taxonomy lacks (proposed as heat-wanted-level). The game is in early access, with an exit planned for Q4 2027.

name: Screeps
summary: A persistent MMO strategy game in which players control colonies only by writing JavaScript that the server runs every tick, directing creeps assembled from body parts to harvest energy, upgrade room controllers, trade, and fight other players' code under a CPU budget.
core_loop: write and commit JavaScript -> each tick the script reads room state and issues orders -> creeps harvest energy for spawns, extensions, and the controller -> controller levels unlock structures -> claim and defend rooms against other players' code -> profile and rewrite code within the CPU limit
design_notes: Screeps removes direct control entirely: the only input to the persistent world is the player's main module, which the server runs once per tick against a fixed snapshot, queuing commands that resolve together at tick end, so the colony keeps acting while the player is offline. Computation is the scarce resource: each tick has a CPU limit (20 without CPU Unlock, otherwise rising with Global Control Level to 300), with unused CPU banked in a 10,000-unit bucket that allows bursts of up to 500. Creeps are designed in code as bodies of up to 50 parts (WORK, CARRY, MOVE, ATTACK, RANGED_ATTACK, HEAL, CLAIM, TOUGH) that set cost, ability, and fatigue, and they die after 1,500 ticks, so a colony is a replacement pipeline. Room Controller Levels 1 to 8 unlock structures and decay if not fed energy, and every player's AI meets the others in shared 50x50 rooms, so strategy is emergent competition between programs. The server is open source and runnable privately.

name: Seaman
summary: A Dreamcast virtual pet in which the player talks through a microphone to a sardonic human-faced fish, managing its tank's heat, water, and food while it matures through five life stages.
core_loop: check the tank each real day -> adjust heat, clean water, and feed -> talk to Seaman through the microphone -> it learns words and asks about the player -> the life stage advances through breeding and die-off -> raise the Frogman generation and release it
design_notes: Yoot Saito built Seaman around speech: a microphone accessory lets the player answer questions and make small talk, early Gillmen repeat the player's words back as gibberish, and the creature's vocabulary grows while it keeps insulting the player. The care loop is sparse but strict, with roughly one check per real day needed to keep it alive, so the game paces itself to the player's calendar. Its life cycle is scripted and harsh: Gillmen fight until two remain, Podfish die after mating, Tadmen eat each other until two remain, and the final Frogmen are released into the wild. Leonard Nimoy narrates the English version as a guide who explains only part of the rules.

name: Second Life
summary: A persistent 3D virtual world in which residents build objects from prims and meshes, script them in the Linden Scripting Language, own land in server-simulated regions, and trade goods and land for Linden Dollars exchangeable for real currency.
core_loop: customize an avatar -> buy or rent land in a region -> build objects from prims and mesh -> script behavior in LSL -> sell creations, land, or services for Linden Dollars -> exchange Linden Dollars on the LindeX
design_notes: Linden Lab describes Second Life as a platform rather than a game: it has no set objective, and almost all content is built and scripted by residents, who keep copyright to it. It is a boundary case included for its user-content pipeline, server-side object scripting, and a virtual currency with a real-money exchange that produced real income for some residents. Each region is simulated on its own CPU core with Havok physics, which caps how many avatars and objects a place can hold.

name: shapez 2
summary: A combat-free factory automation game in which the player builds multi-level factories on space platforms that cut, rotate, stack, and paint layered geometric shapes and deliver them to a central Vortex to meet escalating milestone and operator goals.
core_loop: read the requested shape code -> extract raw shapes from asteroids -> cut, rotate, stack, and paint on belts across levels -> deliver to the Vortex -> earn platform units and research -> build bigger platforms and train networks
design_notes: shapez 2 removes enemies, money, and building costs (all buildings are free) and keeps only the throughput puzzle: the product is an abstract shape of up to four layers of four quadrants, each part with a type and one of nine colors, written as a shape code. Parts obey a support rule (no floating pieces) and crystals shatter when cut from or stacked onto other crystals, so processing order is part of the puzzle. Space is the scarce resource: machines sit on space platforms whose count is limited by Platform Units earned from goals, and platforms connect through edge notches, space belts, and colored train lines whose routing is set per color at splitters. After the fixed milestones, operator goal lines grow exponentially in cost per level (for example 15,000 shapes at 18% growth), turning the endgame into scaling a design rather than designing a new one.

name: Silent Hunter III
summary: A World War II U-boat sim with a dynamic campaign that generates convoys and escorts, manual torpedo targeting, and a persistent crew that gains rank, experience, and morale across patrols.
core_loop: receive a patrol grid -> transit under time compression -> detect contacts -> identify the target and solve speed, angle on the bow, and gyro angle -> fire torpedoes -> evade escorts -> return to base and promote crew
design_notes: The campaign engine generates convoys, destroyer escorts, and task forces in each patrol area rather than scripting engagements, so a career starting between 1939 and 1943 is a sequence of unplanned encounters. Realism settings scale the procedure: at the hardest, the player identifies class and nationality and computes speed, angle on the bow, and gyro angle; with manual targeting off a Weapons Officer solves the problem while approach geometry still matters. Crew members persist between patrols with rank, experience, morale, and decorations.

name: SimAnt
summary: A Maxis ant-colony simulation in which the player controls one yellow ant that lays trails and recruits nestmates while managing a black colony's castes against a rival red colony, predators, and the household.
core_loop: steer the yellow ant -> lay trails and recruit followers to food or the red nest -> colony grows under caste allocation -> fight the red colony and survive hazards -> send young queens and drones to found new nests -> take the yard and drive out the humans
design_notes: Will Wright drew on Hölldobler and Wilson's The Ants to show emergence: individual ants follow simple rules, and the player's main lever on the colony is the trail field that other ants follow, not orders. The player embodies one ant and can swap into any other, which pairs a direct-avatar view with colony-level allocation of workers, soldiers, and breeders. Rain washes away trails and floods nests, and lawnmowers, bug spray, spiders, and antlions kill ants, so the environment erodes the information the player lays down. Trail-following agents are not yet a mechanic in the taxonomy (proposal stigmergic-trails).

name: SimCity
summary: The city builder in which a mayor zones residential, commercial, and industrial land, lays power and roads, and sets taxes while grid maps of land value, crime, pollution, and traffic drive where the city grows.
core_loop: zone residential, commercial, and industrial land -> connect roads and power -> RCI demand and land value grow zones -> collect taxes each year -> fund police, fire, and roads -> respond to crime, pollution, traffic, and disasters
design_notes: Will Wright grew the game out of the map editor he built for Raid on Bungeling Bay and drew its model from Jay Forrester's Urban Dynamics. The simulation is a set of coarse grid maps (land value, crime, pollution, traffic density, police and fire effect) recomputed in passes, plus three RCI demand valves that integrate city-wide balance; a zone grows when its local score plus the valve passes a random test. The 2008 GPL release as Micropolis made these update rules, including crime = 128 - land value + density - police effect, inspectable.

name: SimCity 2000
summary: The isometric sequel to SimCity that adds terrain elevation, an underground layer of water pipes and subways, separate zone tax rates, bonds, ordinances, and power plants that age out.
core_loop: shape terrain and zone light or dense residential, commercial, industrial land -> lay power lines, water pipes, roads, and rail -> demand and land value grow zones -> set per-zone tax rates, ordinances, and bonds -> fund schools, hospitals, police, and fire -> rebuild aging plants
design_notes: SimCity 2000 keeps the original's grid-map model but adds a second plane: an underground view for water pipes, subways, and road tunnels, so infrastructure is laid on a separate layer from zoning. Finance gains levers (three tax rates, ordinances, bonds), and most of the nine power plant types have limited lifespans, so replacement becomes a recurring capital cost. Yearly newspapers built from city state replace the score screen, and extreme deficit spending ends the game.

name: SimCity (2013)
summary: A SimCity reboot built on the agent-based GlassBox engine, in which agents carry workers, power, water, and goods between buildings and small cities share a region over an always-online connection.
core_loop: zone along roads -> GlassBox agents carry workers, goods, power, water, and sewage between buildings -> specialize the city in industries such as manufacturing, education, or tourism -> trade surpluses and share services with region neighbors -> pool resources into Great Works
design_notes: GlassBox replaces statistical maps with units that hold resource bins and agents that move resources between them, so a house holds a count of people and food, water travels as units, and traffic jams are the visible sum of commuting agents. Agents take the first available job and the first empty home rather than keeping persistent lives, and vehicles take the shortest route instead of the least loaded one, which players read as pathfinding errors. Cities were smaller than earlier games by design, and region play links them asynchronously through shared services, trade, and Great Works.

name: SimCity 4
summary: A city builder in which several cities share a region map and trade utilities, while zones develop by density and wealth level and a commute model routes trips across roads and transit.
core_loop: terraform in God mode -> zone residential, commercial, industrial land at a density and connect roads -> wealth-level demand and desirability grow buildings -> set taxes and per-building service funding -> trade power, water, and garbage with neighbor cities -> grow the region
design_notes: SimCity 4 splits each zone type by wealth level, so demand and desirability are tracked per class and neighborhoods can decay or gentrify as conditions change. Cities of 1 to 4 km per side sit in a region and exchange water, electricity, and garbage disposal through neighbor deals, letting several specialized cities depend on each other; this single-player region has no exact match in the taxonomy (see run proposal). Its commute model drew praise from urban planner Jeff Speck, and the Building Architect Tool (2004) sustained a content community for over two decades.

name: SimEarth
summary: A planetary god game built on James Lovelock's Gaia hypothesis in which geology, atmosphere, climate, life, and civilization models interact over billions of years under the player's parameter changes and interventions.
core_loop: set geological, atmospheric, and biological rates -> climate and biomes evolve -> taxa spread, mutate, and diversify -> one sapient species advances through seven ages -> pollution, war, and disasters feed back on climate -> spend energy on interventions
design_notes: Will Wright and Fred Haslam built SimEarth with James Lovelock as adviser, and its models encode Gaian feedback: volcanic dust cools the planet, warming melts ice caps and raises seas, and life alters atmospheric gas fractions shown to three decimal places. The player mostly acts through control panels that set rates such as continental drift, reproduction, and mutation, plus energy-priced interventions (50 units per terrain square, 500 per terraforming device), so play is closer to tuning coupled systems than to directing agents. Scenarios include Daisyworld, Lovelock's minimal model of temperature regulation by daisy color, and terraforming Mars and Venus.

name: SimLife
summary: A Maxis artificial-life toy in which the player edits plant and animal genes, landscape, and the world's physical parameters, then watches food chains and evolution play out.
core_loop: design species genes and world physics -> plants grow and animals eat, breed, and mutate -> populations boom, crash, or go extinct -> read graphs -> edit genes or environment and run again
design_notes: Designed by Ken Karakotsios, SimLife moves the player's control point down to the genome: plant and animal species are edited gene by gene, and the world's physical parameters can be changed, so the toy is about running ecological and evolutionary experiments rather than pursuing goals. Where SimEarth aggregates taxa into planetary stocks, SimLife works at the scale of a landscape and its individual species, mixing exclusive designed animals such as the Killer Penguin and Monkeyphant with player-made ones. Direct gene editing matches the genome-modification proposal from run catalog-ge.

name: SimTower
summary: A skyscraper management game in which the player stacks offices, condos, hotels, and shops and designs elevator service so tenants on daily routines do not wait long enough to stress out and leave.
core_loop: build floors, lobbies, and elevators -> place offices, condos, hotels, and shops -> tenants travel by elevator on daily routines -> long waits raise stress and drive tenants out -> rent and population raise the star rating -> unlock new facilities
design_notes: SimTower turns a building into a vertical transit problem: standard elevators span up to 30 floors and express elevators the full height, so the player designs shafts, sky lobbies, and stops to keep queues short as the tower grows toward 100 floors above ground and 9 below. Tenant stress, not money alone, gates the star rating from one to five and finally the Tower rating, which needs a cathedral on top. Events such as a terrorist bomb ransom, VIP visits that can unlock a star, fires, and pests interrupt the routine.

name: SnowRunner
summary: An off-road trucking sim in which the player hauls cargo across mud, snow, and water whose surfaces deform under each truck's weight and tires, upgrading a fleet to reach harder terrain.
core_loop: take a delivery or repair task -> pick truck, tires, and attachments -> drive into deforming mud, snow, or water -> recover when stuck -> deliver cargo -> earn money and rank -> unlock upgrades and new trucks
design_notes: Terrain is the antagonist: mud, snow, and water respond to vehicle weight, speed, and momentum, so route choice and tire type matter more than speed, and optional timed contests pay more for faster completion. The physics engine is the one Pavel Zagrebelnyy built for MudRunner, the sequel to Spintires. Mechanical upgrades such as snorkels and chain tires are gated behind progress thresholds, and up to four players can share a map.

name: Songs of Syx
summary: A low-fantasy city builder in which tens of thousands of individually simulated citizens and slaves of several races live in a growing city-state whose armies of up to 50,000 units fight real-time battles.
core_loop: lay out houses, streets, and workshops -> tens of thousands of citizens and slaves work, worship, and seek their desires -> appoint nobles to run the realm -> supply and train armies -> fight real-time battles -> trade, ally, or conquer neighboring kingdoms
design_notes: Songs of Syx scales individual simulation to city size: each of tens of thousands of citizens and slaves has a race, religion, fears, and desires, and each soldier in battles of up to 50,000 units needs supplies. Nobles can be appointed or imported to manage the kingdom but may try to usurp the player. The game has been in early access since September 2020 with no fixed 1.0 date.

name: Space Engineers
summary: A voxel sandbox where players mine asteroids and planets and build ships and stations block by block, with every block carrying mass, inertia, power needs, and damage under Newtonian physics.
core_loop: mine ore from voxel asteroids and planets -> refine and assemble components -> weld blocks into ship or station grids -> power and pilot under inertia -> collide, fight, or deform -> repair and redesign
design_notes: Space Engineers treats a ship as a grid of blocks where each block has mass, inertia, and hit points, and functional blocks (thrusters per direction, gyroscopes, reactors, cockpits) decide whether it can move at all; there is no ship stat sheet apart from the blocks. Collisions and weapons deform or destroy individual blocks, and terrain is editable voxels, so construction, mining, and damage share one physical model. Survival mode adds a refine-assemble production chain and suit oxygen and energy, and an in-game programmable block lets players automate ships with scripts.

name: Space Haven
summary: A spaceship colony sim in which the player builds a ship tile by tile and keeps a crew with needs, moods, and relationships alive inside a tile-based simulation of oxygen, CO2, heat, and power.
core_loop: build the ship tile by tile -> balance oxygen, CO2, temperature, and power -> crew work and meet needs -> jump through hyperspace to a new sector -> mine, salvage derelicts, trade, or fight factions -> grow the ship and crew
design_notes: Bugbyte describes it as combining RimWorld-style emergent storytelling with a tile-based gas simulation, and names RimWorld, Dwarf Fortress, Spacebase DF-9, and Oxygen Not Included as inspirations. The ship is both the base and the vehicle, so layout choices (a bed beside the ship core disrupts sleep) and life support are coupled to combat, where fire, smoke, gas, and hull breaches cascade through the same simulation. Early access began in May 2020 and 1.0 shipped in May 2026.

name: SpaceChem
summary: A programming puzzle game in which the player lays out instruction paths for two waldos in grid reactors that grab, bond, rotate, and split atoms into target molecules, with each solution scored on cycles, reactors, and instructions against global histograms.
core_loop: read the input and output molecules -> place waldo paths and instruction icons in a 10x8 reactor -> run and debug collisions -> meet the output quota -> compare cycles, reactors, and instructions on histograms -> optimize or move on
design_notes: SpaceChem made the program itself the factory: each 10x8 reactor holds two waldos, red and blue, programmed independently or synchronized by instruction icons laid on the grid, and multiple reactors connect on a planet-surface pipeline so one reactor's output feeds another. Execution is deterministic, so a solution either produces the quota or deadlocks or collides, and success is followed by global histograms of cycles, reactors, and instructions that Zach Barth designed to show where a solution sits without the intimidation of a ranked leaderboard. Each planet ends in a defense level where production must keep pace with an attacker. Barth expanded the manipulator puzzles of his 2008 Flash game The Codex of Alchemical Engineering, and the instruction-grid plus histogram template recurs across Zachtronics' later games. ResearchNet let players share puzzles.

name: Species: Artificial Life, Real Evolution
summary: A solo-developed evolution simulator in which creatures defined by numeric genes mutate, breed, and speciate in real time across a 3D world while the player observes, edits the gene pool, and alters climate.
core_loop: creatures feed, pay energy costs, and reproduce -> offspring genomes mutate -> environment and rovers decide who eats and who starves -> trait averages drift and lineages split into species -> player edits genes, climate, or triggers ice ages and floods -> watch the clade diagram branch
design_notes: Species, built by a single developer known as Quasar, simulates evolution with no fitness function: genes are numbers, most mutations add a random value in [-1, 1] scaled by a background mutation rate and radiation, and survival is whatever the body and environment allow. Energy costs come from analyzing each creature's skeleton for internal forces and torques, so morphology has a physical price, and creatures can eat only what their head reaches. Species are not predefined: a species is a population that can interbreed within a genetic distance, and it splits only when intermediate forms die out, which the clade diagram records. Species defined at runtime by genetic distance are not yet a mechanic in the taxonomy (proposal runtime-speciation). A free alpha (0.4.0) was public from 2012, and the Steam Early Access build from 2018 has not reached 1.0.

name: Spore
summary: A five-stage game in which the player guides a species from cell to galactic empire, building its body, vehicles, and buildings in part-based editors whose creations are shared automatically through the Sporepedia.
core_loop: eat to earn DNA points -> edit body parts to change abilities -> befriend or fight other species -> stage completes and grants consequence traits -> next stage changes the rules -> colonize and terraform planets -> creations upload to the Sporepedia and populate other players' galaxies
design_notes: Spore's evolution is player design rather than selection: body parts bought with DNA points set speed, attack, and social abilities directly, and nothing is inherited by differential survival. Its distinctive system is the part-based editors (18 share one interface) whose creations are stored as compact descriptions of a few kilobytes and reconstructed procedurally, which let Maxis upload every creation and redistribute them as the inhabitants of other players' galaxies (over 100 million by May 2009). Each of the five stages swaps in a different genre's rules, and play style in each stage assigns consequence traits that carry forward.

name: Stardew Valley
summary: A farming and life sim in which the player restores an inherited farm over four 28-day seasons, splitting a daily energy budget among crops, animals, mining, fishing, and friendships with Pelican Town's residents.
core_loop: plan the day -> spend energy watering, harvesting, mining, or fishing -> sell crops and artisan goods -> buy seeds, tools, and buildings -> gift and talk to villagers -> complete Community Center bundles -> new areas and seasons open
design_notes: Eric Barone built Stardew Valley alone over about five years in response to Harvest Moon, keeping its seasonal crop calendar and town relationships while leaving the long-term structure open-ended. Each day is bounded by an energy bar refilled each morning and a clock that forces sleep, so play is a daily allocation problem across farming, foraging, fishing, mining, and socializing. Friendship is a point stock (250 points per heart, 10 hearts for most villagers) that loses 2 points per day without conversation and accepts two gifts per week, with birthday gifts worth eight times as much. Community Center bundles make collection the main progression gate.

name: Stationeers
summary: A first-person space station survival game whose core is an atmospheric simulation of gas mixtures, pressure, temperature, and combustion that the player must engineer with pipes, power, and programmable logic.
core_loop: land with a starter kit -> mine and smelt ore -> build an airtight frame -> pipe, filter, and heat a breathable atmosphere -> power and automate with logic chips -> expand while fixing pressure, fire, and temperature failures
design_notes: The atmosphere is the main simulated system: each sealed volume and pipe network carries a mix of gases with temperature and pressure, so heating a room raises its pressure, mixing fuel and oxygen can burn or explode, and a pressure difference across a wall can blow it out. Survival needs are deliberately front-loaded; later play is building plant that keeps the atmosphere stable, then automating it with IC10 chips programmed in an assembly language. The game has been in early access since 2017.

name: Stellaris
summary: A real-time-with-pause space 4X and grand strategy game in which the player designs a species and empire, expands across a procedurally generated hyperlane galaxy from 2200, manages pops, jobs, ethics-based factions, and research card draws, and faces late-game crises.
core_loop: survey systems with science ships -> claim systems and colonize planets -> build districts that create jobs for pops -> draw research cards and build fleets -> negotiate or fight neighboring empires -> survive the late-game crisis
design_notes: Stellaris combines a space 4X opening (survey, claim, colonize) with Paradox grand strategy systems: real time with pause, internal factions, and event chains. Its research model replaces a visible tree with weighted random card draws, so two runs of the same empire research in different orders. Hyperlane-only travel turns the galaxy into a graph with chokepoints. Henrik Fahraeus named Star Control II, Master of Orion II, and Europa Universalis IV as roughly equal influences.

name: Subnautica
summary: An underwater survival game on an ocean planet where the player manages oxygen, food, and water while crafting tools, submersibles, and bases to explore deeper and escape.
core_loop: dive from the lifepod -> gather resources and recover blueprints -> craft tools, vehicles, and base modules -> manage oxygen, food, and water -> dive deeper into new biomes and story sites -> build the means to escape the planet
design_notes: Included as a boundary case: the map, story, and progression are hand-authored, and the simulated layer is a set of survival meters plus base power and fauna behavior. Oxygen is the distinctive meter because it ties survival to depth and distance from air, making range a resource. Mode settings remove meters to change genre: Freedom drops hunger and thirst, Creative drops all depleting stats, and Hardcore adds permanent death without low-oxygen warnings.

name: Suck Up!
summary: A voice-controlled comedy game in which the player, as a disguised vampire, talks AI-driven townspeople into letting them inside, with each resident's replies generated by a language model from its personality and the player's words.
core_loop: pick a disguise -> knock on a resident's door -> speak a pitch aloud -> the model replies in character and weighs trust -> get invited in and feed, or get refused -> next house
design_notes: At runtime a language model plays each resident: the player's spoken words go to a hosted model (the Steam page lists ChatGPT from OpenAI; the December 2023 terms name GPT 3.5 and Llama 2 and meter use in tokens) along with the resident's authored personality, and its reply, delivered in voiced audio, decides whether the player has earned entry. The challenge is social engineering against a model that has been told to be suspicious, so disguises (knight, superhero, a previous victim) work as context that changes the model's judgment. Players author new residents' personalities and whole neighborhoods and share them on Steam Workshop. It is a boundary case: the persuasion is judged by the model rather than by a simulated social state.

name: Surgeon Simulator
summary: A physics comedy surgery game in which the player controls one hand with separate finger keys to perform transplants on the patient Bob before his vital signs fail.
core_loop: pick a procedure -> move the hand and press finger keys to grab tools -> cut, break, and remove body parts -> place the new organ -> keep Bob alive -> score and time
design_notes: Made in 48 hours at the 2013 Global Game Jam, the game turns control difficulty into the content: the mouse moves the hand, a mouse button rotates or lowers it, and A, W, E, R, and Space close individual fingers, a scheme modeled on Jurassic Park: Trespasser. Tools and organs are rigid bodies, so most outcomes come from collisions and dropped objects rather than authored surgical steps. Medicine is a comic frame with a thin vital-sign model; a heart rate at zero requires charging the defibrillators. Included as a boundary case for embodied control.

name: Surviving Mars
summary: A Mars colony city builder in which drones build power, water, and oxygen networks before colonists with traits arrive in domes, while research, Earth sponsors, and dust storms, meteors, and cold waves shape survival.
core_loop: land rockets with drones and prefabs -> drones build power, water, and oxygen infrastructure -> build domes and bring colonists from Earth -> colonists' traits, comfort, and sanity drive work and stability -> research and export rare metals for funding -> weather disasters and Mysteries
design_notes: Surviving Mars splits construction from population: drones working within range of hubs build and maintain everything, and colonists arrive only after domes have power, water, and oxygen. Colonists carry traits, flaws, and specializations and track morale, comfort, sanity, and health, so dome services decide whether they work, turn Earthsick, or rebel. Mysteries layer authored storylines (plagues, rival corporations, AI revolts, alien contact) on top of disasters such as dust storms, meteors, and cold waves.

name: Suzerain
summary: A text-based political narrative game in which the player, as newly elected President Anton Rayne of Sordland, makes dialogue and policy choices across one term that shift the budget, foreign alignment, and constitutional reform toward one of several endings.
core_loop: read briefings and dialogue -> choose responses and policy decisions -> budget, alignment, and story flags update -> later options open or close -> reach an ending and a political-compass result
design_notes: Suzerain is mostly authored text, about 450,000 words, in which choices are recorded as state: the budget and accumulated decisions gate later dialogue options and endings. It is a boundary case included for how a political game can run on dilemma choices and state-gated story branches rather than an equation network. The ending screen places the player on an in-universe political compass computed from choices made across the term.

name: Tamagotchi
summary: A 1996 keychain virtual pet whose hunger, happiness, and training meters run on a real-time clock, and whose care quality determines which adult form it grows into and how long it lives.
core_loop: pet calls for attention -> feed a meal or snack, play, scold, clean, or give medicine -> meters and care history accumulate -> pet ages after each sleep -> care history selects its next form -> it lives on or dies
design_notes: Aki Maita and Akihiro Yokoi reduced a pet to three meters (Hunger, Happy, Training) plus droppings and sickness on a three-button LCD device that runs continuously; early units could pause only through the clock settings. Meals fill Hunger, snacks and a minigame raise Happy but excess snacks cause illness, scolding when the pet calls for attention fills Training, and uncleaned droppings lead to sickness shown by a skull. Each life stage lasts a set number of days and age advances when the pet wakes, and care quality selects the adult character, turning care history into a visible outcome (proposed as care-dependent-development).

name: Teardown
summary: A heist and destruction game set in fully destructible voxel levels where the player plans a route by cutting, smashing, and driving through structures, then races a 60-second alarm timer to grab the targets.
core_loop: survey the level -> cut, blast, and ram a route through voxel structures -> stage vehicles and ramps -> trigger the alarm by taking a target -> grab the rest along the planned path before the timer ends
design_notes: Every object is made of small voxels with material types (wood, plaster, brick, metal, glass), and disconnected chunks become rigid bodies that fall, roll, and burn, so geometry is a resource the player spends. The design separates an unlimited planning phase from a timed execution phase: picking up a connected target starts a 60-second alarm, so the player engineers shortcuts with tools, explosives, and vehicles before the first grab. Materials resist tools differently, and fire spreads through wood, which turns construction knowledge into route planning.

name: Terra Nil
summary: A reverse city builder in which the player places machines to clean toxic soil, restore water, and grow biomes on a barren map, then recycles every building and leaves.
core_loop: place wind turbines on rock -> power toxin scrubbers that clean soil -> irrigate and pump water into riverbeds -> upgrade to grow wetlands, meadows, and forest -> attract animals and restore weather -> recycle every building and leave
design_notes: It inverts the city-builder loop: growth is measured in restored tiles rather than population, and points earned per restored tile are the only currency for further buildings, so efficient placement compounds. The final step requires recycling all infrastructure to build an airship and leave, so a layout must be removable as well as productive. Subgenre is set to city-builder because its lineage is placement and budget puzzles rather than population or evolution modeling. It began as a Ludum Dare 45 entry in October 2019.

name: The Farmer Was Replaced
summary: A programming game in which the player writes Python-like code for a farming drone on a grid farm, where every operation costs simulated ticks, and harvests crops to buy unlocks for language features, farm size, more drones, and new crops.
core_loop: write a drone program -> execute it on the farm grid -> plant, water, and harvest crops -> spend harvests on unlocks -> new language features and crops change what code is worth writing -> optimize for speed and leaderboard times
design_notes: The Farmer Was Replaced teaches programming by making farm labor too slow to do any other way: the drone does nothing unless code tells it to, and the language itself is unlocked piecemeal (loops, variables, functions, lists, dictionaries) with farm expansion and new crops. Execution is metered in simulated ticks rather than real CPU: literals and assignment are free, arithmetic and getters cost 1 tick, and a successful move() costs 200, so optimization means reducing drone actions more than reducing statements. Crops add algorithmic puzzles: polyculture companions requested within three moves multiply yield, harvesting the sunflower with the most petals (out of at least ten) gives eight times the power that doubles drone speed, and mazes and dinosaurs need search-style code. Leaderboards run the player's program as fixed-start simulations totaling at least two hours and score the average time. Code lives in .py files that external editors can edit.

name: The Incredible Machine
summary: A Rube Goldberg puzzle game in which the player places supplied parts such as balls, ropes, pulleys, belts, and animals into a level so that a deterministic physics run completes a simple goal.
core_loop: read the puzzle goal -> place the supplied parts among fixed objects -> start the machine -> watch the chain reaction -> adjust positions until the goal triggers
design_notes: Each puzzle fixes some objects in a side-view scene and hands the player a small inventory of parts; the solution is a chain reaction where each part triggers the next, such as a ball dropping on a seesaw that frees a mouse that runs toward cheese. The physics engine models gravity and air pressure as global settings and has no random number generator, so a design behaves the same on every run and solutions are verifiable. A freeform mode exposes all parts so players can make puzzles for others.

name: The Long Dark
summary: A first-person wilderness survival sim set in frozen northern Canada where the player manages warmth, calories, thirst, fatigue, and afflictions against cold, weather, and wildlife.
core_loop: explore a frozen region -> scavenge, hunt, and harvest -> manage calories, thirst, fatigue, and warmth -> weather, night, and wildlife threaten condition -> craft, repair, and shelter -> survive another day until death
design_notes: Survival mode has no zombies or authored goal; the cold, wildlife, and dwindling supplies are the opposition, and death deletes the save. All needs feed a single condition stock: an empty warmth bar drains condition about 20% per hour while empty hunger or fatigue drain about 1% and thirst 2%, so cold is the fast killer and food is the slow one. Time is treated as the scarce resource because every action costs calories and in-game hours. The episodic Wintermute story mode has no permadeath.

name: The Powder Toy
summary: An open-source falling-sand sandbox where hundreds of elements interact cell by cell under simulated air pressure, heat, gravity, and electricity.
core_loop: paint elements onto the grid -> unpause the simulation -> watch particles fall, flow, burn, and react under pressure, heat, and electricity -> adjust or add elements -> save and share the build
design_notes: The Powder Toy combines a per-particle falling-sand layer with coarser fields for air pressure, air velocity, and heat, so explosions push air, air moves powders, and temperature thresholds change element states such as ice to water to steam.
